lessons.title: Outbreaks, resistant organisms, and the isolation cart
lessons.body:
## When one case becomes an outbreak

An **outbreak** is simply more cases than expected for that place and that time. Two patients on one hallway with the same resistant organism in the same week is enough to start asking questions, and infection prevention would rather hear about it early and be wrong.

The response has a shape. Infection prevention writes a **case definition**, builds a **line list** of who, where, when, and which organism, looks for what the cases share, and then changes something: cohorting, dedicated equipment, enhanced cleaning, active surveillance swabs, restricting transfers, or excluding staff from work.

Your part is small and load-bearing. You notice the pattern, you report it, and you do not quietly break precautions because the department is slammed.

## The organisms that drive it

**Multidrug-resistant organisms (MDROs)** are not more virulent than their ordinary cousins. They are harder to treat, so an infection that would have been a week of antibiotics becomes a month, or becomes untreatable.

| Organism | Short version |
|---|---|
| MRSA | Resistant *Staphylococcus aureus*; skin, wounds, blood |
| VRE | Vancomycin-resistant *Enterococcus*; gut, urine, blood |
| ESBL | Gram-negatives that destroy most penicillins and cephalosporins |
| CRE | Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales; the last-line drugs fail |
| MDR *Acinetobacter* | Survives on dry surfaces for weeks; ICU and trauma |
| *Candida auris* | A yeast that colonizes skin, spreads on equipment, resists many disinfectants |

*Candida auris* deserves its own paragraph. It lives on skin rather than in the gut, transfers on blood pressure cuffs, thermometers, and bed rails, survives on surfaces for weeks, and shrugs off several common quaternary disinfectants. It needs contact precautions, a single room, dedicated equipment, and a disinfectant specifically rated against it.

## Cleaning that actually kills what is there

The EPA publishes lists of registered products by target. The three that matter to you:

- **List K** for *C. difficile* spores, which in practice means a bleach-based product, usually about `1:10` household bleach or a commercial equivalent, with a typical wet contact time of `4 minutes`.
- **List G** for norovirus.
- **List P** for *Candida auris*.

A quaternary ammonium wipe, the everyday purple-top, is not on any of those lists. It is fine for a routine room and useless against spores.

Cleaning is also two steps, not one. **Clean first, then disinfect.** Organic material, dried blood, stool, and sputum physically block the disinfectant from reaching the surface, so a visibly dirty surface gets wiped clean, then wiped again with fresh product for the full contact time.

## The isolation cart

The cart lives **outside** the room, not inside, because anything inside a precaution room is contaminated. It holds gowns, gloves in every size, surgical masks, fit-tested N95s in the sizes your staff actually wear, face shields, hand sanitizer, and red regulated-medical-waste bags.

Check and restock it at the start of your shift. A cart with no size-large gowns at 0300 is the reason someone walks in ungowned.

**Regulated medical waste**, the red bag, is for items saturated or dripping with blood or other potentially infectious material, or that would release it if squeezed. A lightly stained 4x4 goes in regular trash. Over-red-bagging is expensive and teaches people the categories do not matter.

## Visitors

Visitors on a precaution room get the same PPE and, more importantly, a `30-second` demonstration of how to put it on and take it off. Handing someone a gown without showing them the doffing order produces a family member who walks down the hall in contaminated gloves.

Screen visitors for fever, cough, rash, and diarrhea, and limit the number in the room during an active outbreak. Visitors do not carry equipment or linens between rooms.

> **Key:** Cohorting means grouping patients who have the **same** organism when single rooms run out. Putting an MRSA patient with a VRE patient does not cohort them; it gives each of them a second organism.

> **On shift:** The equipment is the vector nobody thinks about. The blood pressure cuff, the pulse oximeter probe, the glucometer, and the ultrasound probe go room to room all shift. Wipe them between every patient or leave them in the room.
keyPoints: An outbreak is more cases than expected; infection prevention responds with a case definition, a line list, cohorting, dedicated equipment, and enhanced cleaning.
MDROs include MRSA, VRE, ESBL producers, CRE, MDR Acinetobacter, and Candida auris, which spreads on equipment and resists many common disinfectants.
EPA List K kills C. diff spores (bleach, about 4 minutes wet), List G covers norovirus, List P covers Candida auris; quaternary wipes cover none of them.
Clean first and then disinfect, because organic material blocks the disinfectant from reaching the surface.
The isolation cart stays outside the room, gets restocked every shift, and visitors get PPE plus a demonstration of how to remove it.

checks.q: Single rooms have run out during a resistant-organism outbreak. Which pairing is acceptable cohorting?
choices: An MRSA patient with a VRE patient
Two patients who both have VRE
A C. diff patient with a patient on droplet precautions for flu
Any two contact precaution patients
checks.why: Cohorting means sharing a room only with someone carrying the same organism. Mixing different organisms simply gives each patient the other's, and mixing precaution categories fails to match the barrier to the route.

checks.q: A room held a patient with C. difficile. Which product finishes the job?
choices: A quaternary ammonium wipe with a 2-minute contact time
70 percent alcohol on all high-touch surfaces
An EPA List K sporicidal, typically bleach-based, kept wet for the labeled time
Soap and water followed by air drying
checks.why: Only sporicidal products on EPA List K kill C. diff spores. Quaternary wipes and alcohol do not, and washing without a registered disinfectant leaves viable spores on high-touch surfaces.

checks.q: A bedside table is visibly smeared with dried stool. What is the correct sequence?
choices: Apply disinfectant once and let it sit for the full contact time
Clean the soil off first, then apply fresh disinfectant for the full contact time
Apply disinfectant, wipe it away, and repeat twice
Cover the area and call environmental services for a terminal clean
checks.why: Organic material physically shields organisms from the disinfectant, so cleaning precedes disinfection. A single application over soil never reaches the surface, and repeated short applications never meet the wet contact time.

lessons.title: When staff get exposed: measles, varicella, pertussis, and TB
lessons.body:
## What counts as an exposure

An exposure is contact with an infectious patient **without the right barrier**, during the period that patient was contagious. That last clause matters, because it often means the exposure happened hours before anyone suspected the diagnosis, in triage, in the waiting room, or in the CT corridor.

When a diagnosis lands late, infection prevention builds a contact list from the chart, the tracking board, and the door badge logs, and calls everyone on it. Answer that call. The interventions have deadlines measured in days.

## Measles

Measles is airborne and it is the most contagious thing you will meet. The virus stays suspended in a room for up to `2 hours` after the patient leaves, so the next patient placed in that room is exposed.

A patient is infectious from `4 days before` the rash appears until `4 days after`. Incubation runs `7 to 21 days`.

- Staff with **presumptive immunity**, meaning documented two doses of MMR, a positive titer, or lab-confirmed prior disease, need nothing.
- Staff without it get **MMR within `72 hours`** of exposure, or **immune globulin within `6 days`** if vaccine is contraindicated.
- Non-immune staff are **excluded from work from day `5` after the first exposure through day `21` after the last exposure**, whether or not they got vaccine. That is more than two weeks off.

> **Key:** Nobody tells a non-immune tech to take seventeen days off for fun. Check your own immunization record now, before a measles case walks in, and fix any gap.

## Varicella

Chickenpox is airborne too, and infectious from `1 to 2 days` before the rash until every lesion has crusted.

Non-immune exposed staff get varicella vaccine within `3 to 5 days`, or VariZIG within `10 days` if vaccine is contraindicated, such as pregnancy or immunosuppression. Work exclusion runs **day `8` through day `21` after exposure**, extended to day `28` if VariZIG was given, because the immune globulin stretches the incubation period.

## Pertussis

Whooping cough spreads by droplet, and the exposure that counts is unprotected close contact with respiratory secretions: suctioning, being coughed on, an unmasked face within a few feet.

Exposed staff get **antibiotic prophylaxis**, usually azithromycin, and **stay at work** as long as they are symptom free. A staff member who develops the cough is excluded until they have completed `5 days` of appropriate antibiotics. Every health care worker gets **Tdap once** regardless of when their last tetanus booster was.

## Tuberculosis

TB exposure is not managed with a drug on day one, because there is nothing to treat yet. It is managed with a test on a clock.

You get a **baseline** test, then a **repeat test `8 to 10 weeks` after the last exposure**, because that is how long it takes for the immune response to become detectable. An interferon gamma release assay blood test is preferred over the skin test in vaccinated populations, because prior BCG vaccination causes false-positive skin tests.

A conversion means **latent TB infection**, not disease. It is treated, commonly with weekly isoniazid and rifapentine for `12 weeks` or daily rifampin for `4 months`, and treating it is how you avoid active TB years later.

## The rest of the list

- **Meningococcus.** Prophylaxis goes only to staff with direct exposure to respiratory secretions, such as intubation, suctioning, or mouth-to-mouth. Standing in the room is not an exposure. A single dose of oral ciprofloxacin `500 mg`, or ceftriaxone `250 mg IM`, or rifampin for two days.
- **Influenza.** Staff with flu stay home until at least `24 hours` after the fever is gone without fever-reducing medication.
- **Scabies.** Skin-to-skin contact with **crusted** scabies, the heavily infested form, gets prophylactic permethrin. Ordinary scabies needs prolonged contact to transmit.

> **On shift:** The single best protection against all of this is masking a coughing patient at the door and moving anyone with a fever and a rash out of the shared waiting room immediately. You control both of those without an order.
keyPoints: Measles hangs in the air for 2 hours after the patient leaves; non-immune staff get MMR within 72 hours and are excluded from work day 5 through day 21.
Varicella: vaccine within 3 to 5 days, VariZIG within 10 days, work exclusion day 8 through day 21, or day 28 if VariZIG was given.
Pertussis exposure means azithromycin prophylaxis with no work exclusion unless symptoms develop, then exclusion until 5 days of antibiotics are complete.
TB exposure is managed by baseline testing plus a repeat test 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure; IGRA avoids BCG false positives.
Meningococcal prophylaxis goes only to staff with direct respiratory secretion exposure, not to everyone who was in the room.

checks.q: A confirmed measles patient occupied triage room 2. A tech with documented two doses of MMR was in the room unmasked. What happens to her?
choices: Immune globulin within 6 days
Exclusion from work day 5 through day 21
Nothing, because two documented MMR doses are presumptive immunity
A repeat titer in 8 to 10 weeks
checks.why: Documented two-dose MMR is presumptive immunity, so no prophylaxis and no work exclusion apply. The exclusion and immune globulin rules are for staff without evidence of immunity, and titers are not part of post-exposure management for the already immune.

checks.q: You suctioned a patient later diagnosed with pertussis. You feel fine. What is the correct management?
choices: Azithromycin prophylaxis and continue working while symptom free
Immediate exclusion from work for 21 days
No action, since you are asymptomatic
Baseline testing now and a repeat test in 8 to 10 weeks
checks.why: Unprotected exposure to respiratory secretions warrants antibiotic prophylaxis, and asymptomatic staff on prophylaxis keep working. The 21-day exclusion belongs to measles and varicella, and the delayed retest belongs to TB.

checks.q: Why is the TB follow-up test done 8 to 10 weeks after exposure rather than immediately?
choices: The laboratory batches specimens every two months
It takes that long for a detectable immune response to develop after infection
Prophylactic antibiotics interfere with earlier testing
Skin tests cannot be repeated sooner than 8 weeks
checks.why: Immune conversion takes weeks, so a test done at the time of exposure only establishes a baseline. The delayed test is what detects new infection, and the baseline is what proves it is new.

lessons.title: Restraints minute by minute: four cases and the chart
lessons.body:
## The first question is always which kind

The federal rules split restraint by **why**, not by what the device looks like. The same soft wrist restraint is governed by two completely different rulebooks depending on the reason it is on.

- **Non-violent, medical restraint** protects a medical device or treatment from a patient who cannot cooperate. Orders renew per hospital policy, typically each calendar day after a fresh assessment.
- **Violent, behavioral restraint** manages dangerous behavior. One-hour face-to-face evaluation, time-limited orders of `4 hours` for adults, `2 hours` for ages `9 to 17`, `1 hour` under age `9`, and continuous monitoring.

## Four cases

**Case 1.** An intubated, sedated `68`-year-old keeps reaching for the endotracheal tube as sedation lightens. Soft wrist restraints go on. This is **medical restraint**. The behavior threatens a device, not a person.

**Case 2.** A `24`-year-old in a psychiatric crisis punches a security officer and is placed in four-point restraints. This is **behavioral restraint**. The one-hour clock starts at application, and the order expires in `4 hours`.

**Case 3.** A `79`-year-old with delirium is climbing over the rail. Staff apply a lap belt she cannot undo. This is a restraint, and because the purpose is to prevent a fall rather than to control violence, most hospitals manage it under the non-violent rules with an order and monitoring. What it is not is a fall precaution you apply on your own.

**Case 4.** A `40`-year-old asks for a wrist restraint so he does not scratch a graft in his sleep, and can remove it himself. That is **not a restraint**, because the patient can release it. Voluntary and self-releasable is the dividing line.

> **Trap:** A side rail, a geri-chair tray table, a tucked-in sheet, and a bed exit alarm can all become restraints depending on whether the patient can get out. The test is not the object. The test is whether the patient can freely remove it.

## What the chart has to show

The chart has to tell a stranger, months later, that everything else was tried and that the patient was watched. Write behavior, not adjectives.

- **The behavior.** Observable and quoted: "swung a closed fist at this tech, struck the IV pole, stated 'I will kill you,'" not "patient agitated."
- **Alternatives tried and their outcome.** Lights dimmed, food offered, family called, security presence, medication offered and refused, each with a time.
- **Type and location** of restraint and the **time of application**, limb by limb.
- **The order:** who gave it, when, and its expiration time.
- **The face-to-face:** who performed it and at what time, within `1 hour`.
- **Every `15-minute` check:** circulation and distal pulses, skin, range of motion of each limb, breathing and airway, position, and the offer of fluids, food, and toileting. Document the offer and the answer, including refusals.
- **Release criteria in behavioral terms:** "will be released when able to follow directions and no longer threatening staff." Not "when calm," which means nothing.
- **Release:** time, behavior at release, and limb-by-limb skin check.
- **Debriefing** with the patient when they are able, and with the team.

## A worked timeline

`2012` restraints applied, all four limbs, order obtained from the provider. `2012` face-to-face clock starts, due by `2112`. `2027` first check documented. `2042`, `2057`, `2112` checks. `2035` face-to-face completed by the provider. `2112` limbs released one at a time for range of motion. `0012` order expires; either a new order and a new assessment, or the restraints come off.

A gap in that column is what an attorney finds. A `15-minute` check documented at `2045` and then nothing until `2140` says nobody was watching for an hour.

## When it goes wrong

Deaths connected to restraint are reportable to CMS. A death that occurs **while a patient is restrained**, or **within `24 hours` of removal**, is reported no later than close of business the **next business day**. A death within `1 week` where restraint plausibly contributed is also reportable. Deaths where the only restraint was soft two-point wrist restraints and there was no seclusion go into an internal log instead.

> **On shift:** Set a timer on your phone for the `15-minute` checks the moment restraints go on. Everyone intends to remember. Nobody remembers at minute forty of a code in the next room.
keyPoints: Restraint category is set by the reason, not the device: protecting a device is non-violent restraint, controlling dangerous behavior is behavioral restraint.
Anything the patient cannot remove themselves is a restraint, including rails, lap belts, and tray tables; self-releasable devices are not.
Documentation must quote observable behavior, list alternatives tried with times, and show every 15-minute check including offers of fluids and toileting.
Release criteria are written in behavioral terms the patient can actually meet, not as 'when calm'.
Deaths during restraint or within 24 hours of removal are reported to CMS by close of business the next business day.

checks.q: A patient asks for a wrist strap he can undo himself so he does not scratch a healing graft overnight. What is this?
choices: A behavioral restraint requiring a 1-hour face-to-face evaluation
A medical restraint requiring a daily order
Not a restraint, because the patient applied it voluntarily and can release it
Seclusion
checks.why: The defining test is whether the patient can freely remove the device. A voluntary, self-releasable strap is not a restraint, so neither the behavioral nor the non-violent order requirements apply.

checks.q: Which restraint note would survive review?
choices: 'Patient agitated and combative, restraints applied for safety.'

'Patient swung a closed fist at this tech and stated he would kill staff. Lights dimmed, food and phone offered, security present, medication offered and refused, all documented with times. Four-point soft restraints applied 2012.'
'Patient uncooperative. Restraints per protocol.'
'Restraints applied PRN for ongoing agitation.'
checks.why: The record must show observable behavior and the less restrictive measures that failed, with times. Adjectives like agitated document nothing, 'per protocol' names no alternatives, and PRN restraint orders are prohibited outright.

checks.q: A patient dies 14 hours after behavioral restraints were removed. What is required?
choices: An internal log entry only
A report to CMS no later than close of business the next business day
A report only if restraint is proven to be the cause
No report, because the restraints were already off
checks.why: Deaths within 24 hours of restraint removal are reportable to CMS by close of business the next business day, regardless of proven causation. The internal log alternative applies only to soft two-point wrist restraints with no seclusion.

lessons.title: Workplace violence: screening, response, and the aftermath
lessons.body:
## Scoring the risk instead of guessing it

Experienced staff say they can feel when a room is about to go bad. That instinct is real, and it is also unevenly distributed, so structured tools exist to make it teachable.

The **Broset Violence Checklist** scores six observable behaviors, each present or absent: confusion, irritability, boisterousness, physical threats, verbal threats, and attacking objects. A score of `0` is low risk. A score of `1` to `2` means take preventive action now. A score above `2` means violence is likely and the team plans for it in advance.

**STAMP** is the ED memory aid for what to watch: **S**taring, **T**one of voice, **A**nxiety, **M**umbling, **P**acing.

The value of either tool is not precision. It is that a score written on the board turns a private hunch into a shared plan.

## Keeping weapons out

Emergency departments that screen find weapons at rates that surprise people. Screening comes in layers, and the layer you own is the last one.

- **Entrance screening**: metal detectors or security wanding at the ED entrance, depending on the facility.
- **Belongings**: for behavioral health patients, patients in custody, and anyone on a psychiatric hold, policy typically requires changing into a gown and a search of belongings with security present and a witness. Clothing, bags, belts, shoelaces, and lighters are secured and inventoried.
- **The room**: a behavioral health safe room has no loose equipment, no cords, no ligature points, no glove boxes to throw, and a door that opens outward with two clear exits from the interview space.
- **Patients brought by police** are not automatically searched by police for a hospital's purposes. Ask.

> **Key:** The most common weapon used against ED staff is not a gun or a knife. It is the patient's own hands and feet, followed by whatever was within reach: an IV pole, a chair, a tray table, a computer on wheels.

## When it happens

Call early. The overhead code for a combative person exists so that six people arrive before someone is hurt, not after. Your job during the response is usually one of three things: clear the area of other patients and visitors, bring the equipment the team asks for, or stay out of the way.

For an active shooter, hospitals modify the usual run, hide, fight guidance, because patients on ventilators cannot run. The added option is **secure in place**: lock or barricade the door, turn off lights, silence phones and alarms, move away from the door and out of the sightline, and stay put until law enforcement physically opens the door. Do not open it for a voice.

## Afterward, which is the part that gets skipped

There is a sequence, and most of it does not happen unless somebody insists.

1. **Get evaluated.** Even for a bite, a scratch, or a head strike that feels minor. A human bite is a contaminated wound and an exposure event.
2. **File the incident report** and, separately, the employee injury report. They are different forms feeding different systems.
3. **Workers' compensation.** In New Jersey, notify your employer promptly; written notice within `90 days` of the incident is the statutory backstop, and the claim covers treatment and lost wages.
4. **The OSHA `300` log.** Any injury needing more than first aid, or causing lost time or restricted duty, is recordable.
5. **You may press charges.** An employer cannot forbid it and cannot retaliate for it. New Jersey treats assault on a health care worker performing their duties as an elevated offense rather than simple assault.
6. **Debrief and peer support.** Within days, not weeks.

## The New Jersey framework

New Jersey's **Violence Prevention in Health Care Facilities Act** requires covered facilities to maintain a violence prevention committee with equal representation from management and frontline staff, to conduct a violence risk assessment, to maintain a written violence prevention plan, to train staff, to keep a record of every violent incident, and to protect employees who report from retaliation.

That log is why reporting a shove that left no mark still matters. The committee cannot act on incidents nobody wrote down.

> **On shift:** After an assault, people around you will say "that's just the ED." It is the single most expensive sentence in this profession. Report it anyway.
keyPoints: The Broset Violence Checklist scores confusion, irritability, boisterousness, physical threats, verbal threats, and attacking objects; above 2 means violence is likely.
STAMP is the ED watch list: staring, tone of voice, anxiety, mumbling, pacing.
Behavioral health and custody patients are gowned and their belongings searched and secured with a witness, in a room with no ligature points or throwable equipment.
For an active shooter in a hospital, secure in place is added to run, hide, fight, because many patients cannot be moved.
After an assault: medical evaluation, incident and injury reports, workers' compensation, the OSHA 300 log, the option to press charges, and a debrief.

checks.q: A patient is irritable, pacing, and has just slammed a tray table against the wall while shouting threats. Using the Broset checklist, what does this suggest?
choices: Score 0, low risk
A score above 2, meaning violence is likely and the team should plan for it now
A score that cannot be assigned without a psychiatric consult
Score 1, requiring only documentation
checks.why: Irritability, boisterousness, verbal threats, and attacking objects are four of the six items, putting the score well above 2. The tool is designed to be scored at the bedside by any trained staff member, not by a consultant.

checks.q: An active shooter code is announced and you are in a room with a ventilated patient. What is the appropriate action?
choices: Disconnect the ventilator and carry the patient to the stairwell
Secure in place: lock or barricade the door, lights off, phones silenced, out of the sightline, and open for no one but law enforcement
Leave the patient and evacuate yourself immediately
Open the door to check the hallway for information
checks.why: Running is not possible with a ventilated patient, so hospitals add secure in place to the standard guidance. Opening the door to look, or to a voice, is how sheltering fails, and disconnecting a ventilator to move is not survivable for the patient.

checks.q: A patient bites a tech's forearm, breaking the skin. The tech says it is minor and wants to keep working. What should happen?
choices: Wash it and continue, documenting at the end of the shift
Medical evaluation now as a contaminated wound and exposure event, plus an incident report and an injury report
An incident report only, since it is a minor injury
Nothing, as human bites do not transmit bloodborne pathogens
checks.why: A human bite that breaks skin is both a high-infection-risk wound and a bloodborne pathogen exposure requiring evaluation on the clock. The incident report and the employee injury report are separate forms feeding different systems, and both are needed.

lessons.title: Patient safety events and what happens after the report
lessons.body:
## A fall with injury

The reflex when you find someone on the floor is to pick them up. Do not.

1. **Stay with them and call for help.** Someone else brings the nurse.
2. **Assess before moving.** Level of consciousness, obvious deformity, pain, head strike, and whether they can move all four limbs. If a head or neck injury is possible, stabilize the head and do not move them until the provider clears it.
3. **Anticoagulation is the question that changes everything.** A patient on warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, or clopidogrel who struck their head needs a CT even when they look perfectly fine, because a bleed can take hours to declare itself.
4. **Vitals, neuro checks, and a full set of documentation.**
5. **Post-fall huddle** at the bedside within minutes: what happened, what contributed, what changes now.

Document what you saw, not what you assume. If nobody watched it, the chart says **"found on the floor,"** not "patient fell." Those are different claims and only one of them is something you witnessed.

## Wrong patient

Wrong-patient errors rarely start at the bedside. They start with a duplicate medical record, two patients with similar names on the same board, a label printed for the previous patient, or a specimen labeled at the workstation instead of in the room.

The defenses are boring and absolute. Label at the bedside in the patient's presence, never in advance, never in a batch, and never from memory. Two identifiers against the armband and against the label, every time, including the fifth tube on the same patient.

> **Trap:** A **wrong blood in tube** error, where the label is right but the blood inside came from someone else, is invisible. Every value looks plausible. It is the mechanism behind fatal transfusion reactions, and the only barrier is the identification you did at the bedside.

## Retained items and elopement

**Retained items** are not only a surgical problem. In an ED the versions are a guidewire left in during central line placement, wound packing that nobody documented and nobody removed, a retained vaginal or nasal pack, and a broken catheter or needle fragment. The fix is counting and documenting what went in so the next person knows what has to come out.

**Elopement** means an at-risk patient leaves without staff knowing. It is not the same as leaving against medical advice, which is a capable adult making a documented choice. At-risk patients are those with dementia or delirium, intoxication, psychiatric holds, children, and patients in custody.

When someone is missing: tell the charge nurse and security immediately, activate the facility's code, search the unit including bathrooms and stairwells, check exits and the parking lot, and notify police if the patient is a danger to themselves. Prevention is what actually works: gowning at-risk patients, one-to-one observation, door alarms, and placing them where they are visible from the desk.

## Medication errors you witness

You do not give medications, but you will be standing there. The things worth knowing:

- **High-alert medications** cause disproportionate harm when they go wrong: insulin, opioids, anticoagulants, and concentrated electrolytes, especially potassium chloride.
- **Look-alike, sound-alike** pairs are a known cause, which is why labels use tall-man lettering such as hydrOXYzine and hydrALAzine.
- If it has already reached the patient, the order is: tell the nurse and provider **now**, monitor the patient, then report. Nobody's first move is the form.

## What happens after the report

A **sentinel event** is a patient safety event causing death, permanent harm, or severe temporary harm. It triggers a **root cause analysis**, a structured hunt for the system flaws behind the error, typically completed within `45 days`, with an action plan attached.

The model behind it is **Swiss cheese**: every layer of defense has holes, and harm happens when the holes line up. That is why the analysis asks what let it through rather than who did it.

New Jersey has its own layer. Under the **New Jersey Patient Safety Act**, facilities report serious preventable adverse events to the Department of Health within `5 business days` of discovery, submit a root cause analysis and corrective action plan within `45 days`, and disclose the event to the patient or family. In exchange, the self-critical analysis documents are protected from discovery, which is what makes honest reporting possible at all.

> **On shift:** Reporting a near miss costs you five minutes and protects a stranger you will never meet. Reporting nothing costs nothing today and guarantees the same hole is still there next month.
keyPoints: After a fall, assess before moving, and CT the head of any anticoagulated patient who struck it even if they look well.
Chart 'found on the floor' for an unwitnessed fall, and hold a post-fall huddle at the bedside within minutes.
Label specimens at the bedside in the patient's presence; wrong blood in tube is undetectable and causes fatal transfusion reactions.
Elopement is an at-risk patient leaving unnoticed, which is different from a capable adult leaving against medical advice.
New Jersey's Patient Safety Act requires reporting serious preventable adverse events within 5 business days and a root cause analysis within 45 days.

checks.q: An 82-year-old on apixaban is found sitting on the floor next to her stretcher. She says she is fine and wants to get up. What is correct?
choices: Help her up and document that she had no injury
Keep her still, call for help, assess before moving, and expect head imaging because she is anticoagulated
Help her up and recheck her in an hour
Document the fall as witnessed since she told you what happened
checks.why: Anticoagulated patients bleed intracranially with a normal initial exam, so imaging is driven by the medication and the mechanism, not by how she looks. Moving before assessment risks worsening an occult injury, and a fall you did not see is documented as found on the floor.

checks.q: Why is a 'wrong blood in tube' error especially dangerous?
choices: The specimen clots faster
The label is correct so nothing looks wrong, and the results are plausible for the wrong person
It always causes hemolysis, which is flagged by the lab
The analyzer rejects it automatically
checks.why: There is no downstream detection: the label matches the order and the values look reasonable, which is how incompatible blood gets transfused. Hemolysis flags and analyzer rejection catch handling problems, not identity errors.

checks.q: Under the New Jersey Patient Safety Act, what is required after a serious preventable adverse event?
choices: Report to the Department of Health within 5 business days and submit a root cause analysis within 45 days
Report to CMS within 24 hours
An internal log entry only
Notification to the medical examiner within 1 hour
checks.why: The Act sets a 5-business-day reporting deadline and a 45-day root cause analysis with a corrective action plan, plus disclosure to the patient or family. The 24-hour CMS rule belongs to restraint deaths and the 1-hour rule to organ procurement referral.

lessons.title: Evacuation and the hospital incident command system
lessons.body:
## Moving patients is dangerous, so the default is not to

Hospitals are built as a series of sealed compartments joined by fire doors, and a modern building is designed to let a fire burn in one compartment while people two doors away stay where they are. That strategy is called **defend in place**, and it is usually the right one, because dragging ventilated, sedated, and post-operative patients down a stairwell injures and kills people.

So the evacuation decision is made by the **incident commander** or the fire officer in charge, not by whoever is closest to the smoke. The one exception is immediate rescue: if a patient is in the room with the fire, you move that patient now and explain later.

## Horizontal first, vertical last

**Horizontal evacuation** moves patients through the fire and smoke doors into the adjacent compartment on the same floor. It is fast, it uses no stairs, and it is usually sufficient.

**Vertical evacuation** goes down the stairs, and is ordered only when the floor itself is untenable. **Never an elevator**, because shafts fill with smoke, power fails, and the car can open on the fire floor.

The equipment for stairs: **stair chairs** for anyone who can sit, **evacuation sleds or mattress sleds** that strap to the bed and slide down the stairs for bedbound patients, and as a last resort the blanket drag or a two-person carry.

### Who goes in what order

1. **Anyone in immediate danger**, regardless of how well they walk.
2. **Ambulatory patients**, because they move themselves and clear the corridor for everyone else.
3. **Wheelchair and assisted patients.**
4. **Non-ambulatory and total-care patients**, who need the most staff per patient.

As you clear each room, **mark the door** with tape or a marked sign so nobody searches it twice, and **keep a written count**. Someone at the assembly point is reconciling names against the tracking board, and an uncounted patient means the search continues while the building burns.

> **Key:** The number that matters at the end is not how fast you moved. It is whether every patient is accounted for by name.

## The oxygen zone valve

The valves in the hallway cut piped oxygen to a section of the department. Closing one during a fire removes the accelerant, and it is sometimes exactly right.

It is also a decision that stops oxygen to every patient behind that valve, including anyone on a ventilator. So: it is closed **only on the order of the person running the response**, and before it closes, someone identifies every patient on piped oxygen in that zone, stages portable cylinders, and puts a bag-valve mask at the bedside of every ventilated patient.

## The hospital incident command system

When an event is bigger than the usual shift, the hospital switches into **HICS**, a standardized command structure that matches how fire and police organize, so agencies can work together.

At the top is the **incident commander**, supported by a **public information officer**, a **safety officer**, and a **liaison officer**. Below that sit four sections:

| Section | Owns |
|---|---|
| Operations | The actual work: clinical care, security, evacuation |
| Planning | Tracking the situation, patients, and resources; writing the plan |
| Logistics | Supplies, equipment, beds, food, communications |
| Finance and administration | Time, cost, claims, procurement |

The rules that affect you directly:

- **Job action sheets.** Every role has a printed card listing exactly what that role does. You are handed one and you work from it.
- **Plain language, no codes.** Outside agencies do not know your color codes.
- **Span of control is `3` to `7` people, ideally about `5`.** If you are supervising twelve, the structure is wrong.
- **The labor pool.** Off-duty staff who come in report to the labor pool for assignment, not to their own unit. Self-deploying to where you think you are needed is how sixty people end up in one hallway.

## Surge and decontamination

Surge capacity comes from decompressing: discharging and transferring the patients who can go, cancelling elective work, and opening pre-designated space.

For a chemical incident, patients are **decontaminated before entry**, because a contaminated patient brought inside contaminates the department and takes it out of service. Removing clothing alone eliminates roughly `80` to `90 percent` of contaminant, and the rest comes off with a water and soap shower. Decon team members wear a protective ensemble with a powered air-purifying respirator.

> **On shift:** Learn two things in your first week that most people never learn: which stairwells are evacuation routes from your zone, and where the evacuation sleds are stored. Both are useless information until the day they are the only useful information.
keyPoints: Defend in place is the default because hospitals are compartmentalized; the evacuation order comes from the incident commander, not from staff at the scene.
Evacuate horizontally through fire doors first, vertically by stairs only if the floor is untenable, and never by elevator.
Order of movement: immediate danger, then ambulatory, then assisted, then total-care patients; mark cleared rooms and keep a written count.
Oxygen zone valves are closed only on command, after staging portable cylinders and bag-valve masks for ventilated patients.
HICS uses an incident commander over Operations, Planning, Logistics, and Finance, with job action sheets, plain language, span of control of 3 to 7, and a labor pool.

checks.q: Smoke is reported in an adjacent compartment and the alarm is sounding. No order has been given. What is the correct default?
choices: Begin vertical evacuation of all patients immediately
Move anyone in immediate danger, close doors, and hold in place pending the incident commander's order
Use the elevators to clear the non-ambulatory patients first
Shut all oxygen zone valves as a precaution
checks.why: Hospitals are designed to defend in place, and moving patients carries its own mortality, so the evacuation order belongs to the incident commander. Elevators are never used, and zone valves are closed only on command because they cut oxygen to ventilated patients.

checks.q: Vertical evacuation has been ordered. Which patient group moves first?
choices: The sickest and least mobile, because they take longest
Patients in immediate danger, then ambulatory patients who clear the corridor themselves
Visitors and family members
Whoever is nearest the stairwell regardless of condition
checks.why: Immediate danger always outranks everything, and ambulatory patients move themselves, freeing staff and clearing the corridor for the slower groups. Starting with total-care patients consumes every available person while dozens who could walk remain in the smoke.

checks.q: You arrive from home during a mass casualty activation. Where do you go?
choices: Directly to the ED, since that is your unit
To the labor pool for assignment
To the incident commander for personal instructions
To the ambulance bay to help unload
checks.why: The labor pool exists so staffing is assigned where it is needed and tracked. Self-deploying to your own unit or the ambulance bay concentrates people in the most visible place, and the incident commander does not assign individuals.

lessons.title: Radiation, MRI, and laser safety when you transport
lessons.body:
## ALARA and the three levers

The governing principle for radiation is **ALARA**, as low as reasonably achievable. There is no threshold below which scatter radiation is known to be harmless, so the goal is always less.

You have exactly three levers:

- **Time.** Less time near the source.
- **Distance.** The strongest one, because of the **inverse square law**: double your distance and the dose drops to one quarter.
- **Shielding.** A lead apron of `0.5 mm` lead equivalent, plus a thyroid collar.

## Portable films in the department

The technologist calls "X-ray" for a reason. If you have no role in the exposure, step out or behind the shield. If you must stay, wear an apron and thyroid collar and stand at least `6 feet` away, and ideally at **`90 degrees` to the beam** on the side of the patient, because scatter is lowest perpendicular to the primary beam.

With a **C-arm** during fluoroscopy, the scatter comes off the patient toward the X-ray tube. The tube belongs **under** the table, so the higher-dose side is low and near the tube. Stand on the image-detector side, step back during the actual fluoroscopy runs, and remember that fluoroscopy time is continuous, not a single snap.

## Your badge and your limits

A **dosimeter badge** is worn at the collar, **outside** the lead apron, so it measures what reaches your unshielded thyroid and eyes.

The occupational whole-body limit is `50 mSv` per year. For a **declared pregnant worker**, the limit for the entire pregnancy is `5 mSv`, with no more than about `0.5 mSv` in any month. Declaring the pregnancy is voluntary and must be in writing, and it is what triggers the lower limit and a fetal badge. An undeclared pregnancy gets no extra protection, because nobody knows to provide it.

> **Trap:** A lead apron left folded or thrown over a rail cracks internally, and a cracked apron shields nothing while looking perfectly fine. Hang it on the rack.

## MRI: the magnet is never off

The single most important fact about MRI: **the magnet is always on.**

The suite is divided into four zones. Zone I is public space. Zone II is where screening and interviews happen. Zone III is restricted and access-controlled, where the field starts to matter. **Zone IV is the magnet room.**

Ferromagnetic objects become projectiles at high speed. Oxygen cylinders, IV poles, stretchers, scissors, stethoscopes, clipboards, pens, hairpins, and floor buffers have all been pulled into magnets. People have died. A steel oxygen cylinder is the classic killer, which is why any oxygen going into Zone IV is in a non-magnetic aluminum cylinder or piped.

Screening is written, and done twice by two people. What matters: pacemakers and defibrillators, cochlear implants, neurostimulators, aneurysm clips, retained metal fragments in the eye from grinding or welding, medication patches with a metallic backing, which can burn, and any implant of unknown type.

### Emergencies in the magnet room

If your patient arrests in the scanner, **you do not bring the crash cart into Zone IV.** You get the patient out of the magnet room to the designated resuscitation area, and the code happens there.

The **quench button** dumps the magnet's liquid helium to kill the field. It is used only when a person is pinned by a ferromagnetic object and cannot be freed. It destroys an expensive magnet, and the released helium displaces oxygen and can frostbite anyone nearby, so quenching is followed by evacuating and ventilating the room.

## Lasers

Where lasers are used, a laser safety officer sets the rules. Three hazards matter to you:

- **Eyes.** Everyone in the room, including the patient, wears eyewear rated for that specific wavelength. Glasses for one laser do not protect against another.
- **Plume.** Laser and electrosurgical smoke contains viable viral particles including HPV, plus carcinogens. It is captured with a smoke evacuator held close to the source, and staff wear high-filtration masks.
- **Fire.** Alcohol-based prep near a laser is a fire, so it is allowed to dry fully or is not used. Airway laser cases use the lowest tolerable oxygen concentration and wet towels around the field.

> **On shift:** Before you push any stretcher toward MRI, empty your own pockets and check the stretcher: oxygen cylinder, trauma shears, penlight, badge clip, and the IV pump. The screening question you skip is the one about yourself.
keyPoints: ALARA works through time, distance, and shielding; the inverse square law means doubling distance quarters the dose.
For portable films stand at least 6 feet away at 90 degrees to the beam; with a C-arm stand on the detector side, away from the tube.
Dosimeters are worn at the collar outside the apron; the annual limit is 50 mSv, but a declared pregnancy drops it to 5 mSv for the whole gestation.
The MRI magnet is always on, Zone IV is the magnet room, and codes are run outside it because the crash cart cannot enter.
Laser safety means wavelength-specific eyewear for everyone, smoke evacuation of infectious plume, and no alcohol prep near the beam.

checks.q: You are standing 3 feet from a portable X-ray exposure and step back to 6 feet. What happens to your dose?
choices: It halves
It falls to one quarter
It is unchanged because you are still in the room
It falls to one eighth
checks.why: The inverse square law means dose falls with the square of distance, so doubling distance from 3 to 6 feet reduces it to one quarter. Halving would require distance alone to be linear, which it is not.

checks.q: A patient in the MRI scanner goes into cardiac arrest. What do you do?
choices: Bring the crash cart into Zone IV and begin compressions in the bore
Press the quench button to shut the magnet off, then resuscitate in place
Remove the patient from the magnet room to the designated resuscitation area and code them there
Wait for the MRI technologist to power down the magnet
checks.why: The crash cart is ferromagnetic and cannot enter Zone IV, and the magnet cannot be switched off, so the patient comes out to the code. Quenching is reserved for a person physically pinned and creates an oxygen displacement hazard of its own.

checks.q: A tech in her first trimester works near fluoroscopy and has not told anyone. What applies to her dose limit?
choices: The 5 mSv gestational limit applies automatically once she is pregnant
The standard 50 mSv annual limit applies, because the lower limit begins only when the pregnancy is declared in writing
She is barred from all radiation areas by federal rule
Her badge automatically alarms at the fetal limit
checks.why: The gestational limit and fetal badge are triggered by a voluntary written declaration, so an undeclared pregnancy is managed under the standard limit. No rule bars pregnant workers from radiation areas, and badges are read after the fact rather than alarming.

lessons.title: Lasting the career: your body, your sleep, and peer support
lessons.body:
## The injuries that end careers are cumulative

The dramatic back injury from one bad lift is real but uncommon. What actually removes people from this work is the slow accumulation: ten thousand small reaches, twists, and static holds over a decade.

The defenses are unglamorous.

- **Neutral posture at the workstation.** Monitor top at eye level, elbows at about `90 degrees`, wrists straight, feet flat. A computer on wheels set for a colleague eight inches taller is a neck injury you take home.
- **Microbreaks.** Thirty seconds of shoulder rolls and a hip hinge stretch every hour beats one long stretch at the end of the shift.
- **The `20-20-20 rule`** for screen strain: every `20 minutes`, look at something `20 feet` away for `20 seconds`.
- **Footwear.** Supportive shoes replaced roughly every `6 months` of full-time floor work, because the midsole compresses long before the tread looks worn.
- **Compression socks** at `15 to 20 mmHg` for the leg swelling and aching that comes from twelve hours of standing.
- **Alternate tasks.** If you have done four straight hours of EKGs, trade for something that uses different muscles.

## Night shift is a physiological problem, not a willpower problem

Your circadian system runs on light, and working nights fights it. Treat that as an engineering problem.

- **Light.** Bright light during the first half of your shift helps you stay alert. **Sunglasses on the drive home** at sunrise prevent the morning light from resetting your clock and making sleep impossible.
- **Caffeine has a half-life of about `5 hours`.** A cup at `0400` still has half its dose on board at `0900` when you are trying to sleep. Stop caffeine about `6 hours` before intended sleep.
- **Naps.** Either about `20 minutes`, short enough to avoid deep sleep, or a full `90 minutes` to complete a cycle. The `45-minute` nap is the worst option, because it wakes you out of slow-wave sleep groggy.
- **Sleep environment.** Blackout curtains, phone off, and a household that understands your sleep is not optional.

**The drive home is the most dangerous part of a night shift.** Being awake `17 hours` impairs performance about as much as a blood alcohol concentration of `0.05 percent`, and `24 hours` awake is roughly `0.10 percent`. If you catch yourself drifting or missing an exit, pull over and sleep, or call someone.

> **Trap:** Eating and drinking are prohibited in patient care areas under the bloodborne pathogen rules, and specimens never share a refrigerator with food. The break room exists because a coffee cup on a workstation is a legitimate exposure route.

## Burnout, compassion fatigue, and moral injury

These get used interchangeably and they are not the same thing.

**Burnout** has three components: emotional exhaustion, depersonalization meaning you stop seeing patients as people, and a collapsing sense of accomplishment. It is a response to chronic workload and lack of control.

**Compassion fatigue**, or secondary traumatic stress, comes from repeated exposure to other people's trauma. It looks like intrusive images, numbing, and dread before shifts.

**Moral injury** is different and more precise: the damage done by being required to act against what you know is right. Holding a patient in a hallway for eighteen hours because there is no bed is not a failure of your resilience. Calling it burnout puts the problem inside you and lets the system that caused it off the hook.

## What actually helps

- **Peer support programs.** Trained colleagues who reach out after hard cases, in models like RISE and Code Lavender. Peer support has better evidence than any single intervention here.
- **The employee assistance program.** Free, confidential, usually several sessions, and it covers things that are not work: finances, legal problems, family.
- **A note on debriefing.** Team debriefs to review the clinical event are useful. Mandatory single-session psychological debriefing, where everyone is required to describe their feelings right after a trauma, has not been shown to prevent PTSD and may make some people worse. Attend, contribute what you want, and use follow-up support rather than treating one session as the treatment.
- **Watch for the specific red flags:** sleep that does not come back after a week, drinking to come down after shifts, avoiding a type of patient, and any thought of self-harm. The `988` Suicide and Crisis Lifeline is `24` hours a day.

> **On shift:** The delayed reaction is the normal one. You will be fine at the time, competent through the whole case, and then be ambushed in the car three days later. That is not weakness or a sign you were unfit; it is the standard timeline.
keyPoints: Career-ending injuries are cumulative: neutral workstation posture, hourly microbreaks, supportive shoes every 6 months, and 15 to 20 mmHg compression socks.
Caffeine has a 5-hour half-life, naps work at 20 or 90 minutes but not 45, and sunglasses on the drive home protect daytime sleep.
Being awake 17 hours impairs you like a blood alcohol of 0.05 percent and 24 hours like 0.10 percent, which makes the post-night-shift drive the real danger.
Burnout is exhaustion from workload, compassion fatigue is secondary trauma, and moral injury is being forced to act against what you know is right.
Peer support and the employee assistance program help; mandatory single-session psychological debriefing does not prevent PTSD.

checks.q: You finish a night shift at 0730 and have a 40-minute drive. You feel alert but have been awake 19 hours. What is the safest plan?
choices: Drive home with the windows down and the radio loud
Drink coffee and drive immediately
Treat the impairment as real: nap before driving, or arrange a ride
Drive but take surface streets instead of the highway
checks.why: At 17 hours awake, performance is impaired comparably to a blood alcohol of 0.05 percent, and feeling alert is an unreliable self-assessment. Air, noise, and route changes do not restore vigilance, and caffeine masks sleepiness without reversing it.

checks.q: A tech says: 'I'm not exhausted. I'm angry. I know what those patients needed and I was made to do something else for eighteen hours.' What is this best described as?
choices: Moral injury
Burnout
Compassion fatigue
Normal shift irritability
checks.why: Moral injury is the harm from being required to act against your own judgment of what is right, and the tell is anger rather than exhaustion. Burnout centers on emotional exhaustion and depersonalization, and compassion fatigue on secondary exposure to others' trauma.

checks.q: Which nap length is the worst choice mid-shift?
choices: 20 minutes
45 minutes
90 minutes
10 minutes
checks.why: A 45-minute nap typically wakes you out of slow-wave sleep, producing the worst grogginess. Short naps stay above deep sleep and a 90-minute nap completes a full cycle, both of which avoid that.

lessons.title: The medical examiner, evidence, and the New Jersey death process
lessons.body:
## Who has jurisdiction

In New Jersey, death investigation runs through the **Office of the Chief State Medical Examiner** within the Department of Health, with county and regional offices doing the actual casework. When a death falls into a reportable category, the body and everything on it belong to the medical examiner's investigation, not to the hospital.

Reportable categories in New Jersey include deaths by violence, whether homicide, suicide, or accident; sudden death in a person who appeared healthy; death not attended by a physician; suspicious or unusual circumstances; poisoning or suspected overdose; occupational injury or disease; death during or related to an operation, procedure, or anesthesia; death in custody or in a public institution; deaths posing a threat to public health; and unidentified remains.

That list swallows most emergency department deaths. Which is why the working assumption is always that it is a medical examiner case until the medical examiner says otherwise.

## Evidence, in practical steps

When clothing must be cut off during a resuscitation, **cut around the holes, never through them.** A bullet hole or a stab defect in fabric carries the size, shape, and residue that tells an examiner the range and the weapon. A trauma shear straight through it destroys that.

- **Paper bags, not plastic.** Plastic traps moisture and lets bacteria degrade biological evidence. Wet or bloody clothing is air dried when possible and always bagged in paper.
- **One item per bag**, sealed, labeled with the patient identifiers, the date and time, the contents, and **your initials across the seal**.
- **Do not shake out clothing**, because trace evidence falls out of it.
- In suspected homicide or firearm deaths, **the hands may be bagged in paper** to preserve residue. Do not wash the hands.
- **Keep the sheets** the patient was lying on. They carry trace evidence too.
- **Chain of custody** means every transfer is documented and signed, from you to the next person, with date and time. Evidence is never left on a counter, and never handed to family.

## Care of the body

Once the medical examiner releases the body or declines the case, post-mortem care proceeds: the body is positioned, identification is verified, and it is tagged. Most facilities use two or three identification tags, typically one on the ankle or toe, one on the shroud or bag exterior, and one on the paperwork.

## Paperwork and timelines

A provider **pronounces** death and records the time. **Certification**, meaning signing the cause of death on the death certificate, is done by the attending physician or by the medical examiner. New Jersey expects the death certificate to reach the local registrar promptly, generally within `24 hours`.

> **Key:** Pronouncement is not certification, and neither one is release. A family asking when they can take him to the funeral home is asking about release, which the medical examiner controls.

## Religion, autopsy, and New Jersey law

Several faiths, including Orthodox Judaism and Islam, hold that the body should be buried quickly and intact, and that autopsy is a desecration. New Jersey law recognizes this: when there is a known religious objection, an autopsy generally may not proceed unless there is a compelling public necessity, such as a suspected homicide or a threat to public health, and the family is given the opportunity to seek a court's decision.

You do not adjudicate any of this. What you do is **hear the objection, say that you will make sure the right people know, and tell the nurse and the provider immediately**, because the timeline is short and the family is trying to meet a burial deadline measured in hours.

## Children

The death of a child is reportable to the medical examiner essentially always, and any concern about abuse or neglect triggers a separate obligation. In New Jersey **every person is a mandatory reporter**, with no exceptions for reporting through a supervisor, and reports go to the State Central Registry at `1-877-NJ-ABUSE`. You report a reasonable suspicion. You do not investigate it and you do not need proof.

> **On shift:** Families in the worst hour of their lives ask small, answerable questions: can I have his wedding ring, where are his glasses, who has his phone. Write the answers down and follow up on them. That is most of what they will remember about the hospital.
keyPoints: New Jersey death investigation runs through the Office of the Chief State Medical Examiner; most ED deaths fall into a reportable category.
Cut clothing around bullet or stab defects, never through them, and bag evidence in paper, one item per bag, sealed and initialed.
Chain of custody documents every transfer with a signature, date, and time; evidence is never left unattended or given to family.
Pronouncement, certification of the death certificate, and release of the body are three different acts, and the medical examiner controls release.
New Jersey honors religious objections to autopsy absent a compelling public necessity, and every person in the state is a mandatory reporter of suspected child abuse at 1-877-NJ-ABUSE.

checks.q: A gunshot victim's shirt must be cut off during resuscitation. What is the correct technique?
choices: Cut along the seams and discard the shirt
Cut around the defects so the holes stay intact, then bag the shirt in paper
Cut through the holes to save time, and document their original location
Leave the shirt on to preserve evidence
checks.why: The size, shape, and residue around a defect carry forensic information that cutting through destroys, and paper bagging prevents moisture from degrading biological evidence. Resuscitation still takes priority, so leaving the shirt on is not the answer.

checks.q: A family tells you their faith forbids autopsy and their father must be buried before sundown. What is your role?
choices: Explain that the medical examiner's authority overrides religious objections
Tell them the autopsy has been cancelled
Acknowledge it, tell the nurse and provider immediately, and make sure the objection is communicated because the timeline is short
Refer them to the funeral home
checks.why: New Jersey law recognizes religious objections to autopsy unless there is compelling public necessity, so the objection must reach the decision makers fast. You neither grant it nor deny it, and deferring to the funeral home wastes hours the family does not have.

checks.q: You suspect that a child's injuries do not match the story you were told. What is required of you in New Jersey?
choices: Tell your charge nurse and let her decide whether to report
Gather more information before reporting anything
Report a reasonable suspicion yourself to the State Central Registry at 1-877-NJ-ABUSE
Report only if the provider agrees
checks.why: New Jersey has universal mandatory reporting, so the duty is personal and cannot be delegated up a chain of command. The standard is reasonable suspicion, not proof, and investigating is the agency's job rather than yours.

cards.front: What is the definition of an outbreak, and what does infection prevention build first?
cards.back: More cases than expected for that place and time. They write a case definition and build a line list of who, where, when, and which organism, then look for what the cases share.

cards.front: Name six multidrug-resistant organisms you will meet in an ED.
cards.back: MRSA, VRE, ESBL-producing gram-negatives, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter, and Candida auris.

cards.front: Why is Candida auris handled differently from other yeasts?
cards.back: It colonizes skin rather than gut, transfers on cuffs, probes, and rails, survives on surfaces for weeks, and resists several common quaternary disinfectants. Single room, contact precautions, dedicated equipment.

cards.front: What do EPA Lists K, G, and P cover?
cards.back: List K is sporicidal for C. difficile, usually bleach at about 1:10 with roughly a 4-minute wet time. List G covers norovirus. List P covers Candida auris.

cards.front: Why is cleaning a two-step process?
cards.back: Organic material such as dried blood, stool, or sputum physically blocks disinfectant from reaching the surface. Clean the soil off first, then apply fresh disinfectant for the full contact time.

cards.front: What does correct cohorting mean when single rooms run out?
cards.back: Grouping patients who carry the same organism. Pairing an MRSA patient with a VRE patient is not cohorting; it simply gives each of them a second organism.

cards.front: Where does the isolation cart live and what is on it?
cards.back: Outside the room, never inside. Gowns, gloves in all sizes, surgical masks, fit-tested N95s in the sizes staff wear, face shields, hand sanitizer, and red regulated-waste bags. Restock every shift.

cards.front: What actually belongs in a red regulated medical waste bag?
cards.back: Items saturated or dripping with blood or other potentially infectious material, or that would release it if compressed. A lightly stained gauze goes in regular trash.

cards.front: What do visitors to a precaution room need beyond the PPE itself?
cards.back: A short demonstration of how to put it on and, more importantly, take it off. Screen them for fever, cough, rash, and diarrhea, and limit numbers during an outbreak.

cards.front: How long does measles virus stay in the air after the patient leaves the room?
cards.back: Up to 2 hours. The next patient placed in that room is exposed, which is why a suspected measles room stays closed after the patient is moved.

cards.front: When is a measles patient infectious?
cards.back: From 4 days before the rash appears until 4 days after it appears. Incubation runs 7 to 21 days, which is why exposure follow-up lasts three weeks.

cards.front: What happens to a non-immune staff member exposed to measles?
cards.back: MMR within 72 hours, or immune globulin within 6 days if vaccine is contraindicated, plus exclusion from work from day 5 after first exposure through day 21 after last exposure.

cards.front: What counts as presumptive immunity to measles for health care staff?
cards.back: Documented two doses of MMR, a positive antibody titer, or laboratory-confirmed prior disease. With it, no prophylaxis and no work exclusion after an exposure.

cards.front: What is the post-exposure management for varicella in a non-immune staff member?
cards.back: Varicella vaccine within 3 to 5 days, or VariZIG within 10 days if vaccine is contraindicated. Work exclusion day 8 through day 21, extended to day 28 if VariZIG was given.

cards.front: What happens after a pertussis exposure?
cards.back: Antibiotic prophylaxis, usually azithromycin, and no work exclusion while symptom free. If the cough develops, exclusion until 5 days of appropriate antibiotics are complete.

cards.front: How is a TB exposure followed, and why the delay?
cards.back: Baseline test now, repeat test 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure, because that is how long a detectable immune response takes. IGRA blood testing avoids BCG false positives.

cards.front: How is latent TB infection treated?
cards.back: Commonly weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine for 12 weeks, or daily rifampin for 4 months. Treating latent infection is how active TB years later is prevented.

cards.front: Who gets meningococcal post-exposure prophylaxis?
cards.back: Only staff with direct exposure to respiratory secretions, such as intubation, suctioning, or mouth-to-mouth. Ciprofloxacin 500 mg once, ceftriaxone 250 mg IM, or rifampin for two days.

cards.front: When can a staff member with influenza return to work?
cards.back: At least 24 hours after the fever has resolved without any fever-reducing medication. Cough alone with no fever is managed with masking per policy.

cards.front: What separates non-violent medical restraint from behavioral restraint?
cards.back: The reason, not the device. Protecting a device or treatment is non-violent, renewed per policy, usually daily. Controlling violent or self-destructive behavior is behavioral, with a 1-hour face-to-face and time-limited orders.

cards.front: What is the single test for whether something counts as a restraint?
cards.back: Whether the patient can freely remove it. A rail, a tucked sheet, a tray table, or a lap belt is a restraint if they cannot; a strap they applied and can undo is not.

cards.front: How should the behavior that justified restraint be charted?
cards.back: Observable and quoted: 'swung a closed fist at this tech, struck the IV pole, stated I will kill you.' Never adjectives like agitated, combative, or uncooperative.

cards.front: What else must the restraint record show besides the behavior?
cards.back: Each alternative tried with a time and outcome, restraint type and location, application time, the order and its expiration, the face-to-face time and performer, every 15-minute check, release criteria, and release details.

cards.front: How should restraint release criteria be written?
cards.back: In behavioral terms the patient can actually meet: 'released when able to follow directions and no longer threatening staff.' Not 'when calm,' which is unmeasurable and never documented as met.

cards.front: An adult is placed in behavioral restraints at 2012. What are the two deadlines?
cards.back: Face-to-face evaluation by 2112, within 1 hour of application. The order expires at 0012, 4 hours later, and a new order with a new assessment is required to continue.

cards.front: Which restraint-related deaths are reported to CMS, and how fast?
cards.back: Deaths while restrained, within 24 hours of removal, or within 1 week where restraint plausibly contributed. Reported by close of business the next business day.

cards.front: What six behaviors does the Broset Violence Checklist score?
cards.back: Confusion, irritability, boisterousness, physical threats, verbal threats, and attacking objects. A score of 1 to 2 means act now; above 2 means violence is likely.

cards.front: What does STAMP stand for?
cards.back: Staring, Tone of voice, Anxiety, Mumbling, Pacing. An ED memory aid for the behaviors that precede violence.

cards.front: What does weapons screening look like for a behavioral health patient?
cards.back: Change into a gown, search and inventory belongings with security present and a witness, and secure clothing, bags, belts, shoelaces, and lighters. Never assume police already searched them.

cards.front: What makes a behavioral health safe room safe?
cards.back: No loose or throwable equipment, no cords, no ligature points, controlled access, and two clear exits from the interview space with a door that does not trap staff.

cards.front: What is 'secure in place' and why do hospitals add it to run, hide, fight?
cards.back: Lock or barricade, lights off, phones silenced, out of the sightline, open for no one but law enforcement. Hospitals add it because ventilated and immobile patients cannot run.

cards.front: What are the six steps after being assaulted at work?
cards.back: Get medically evaluated, file the incident report, file the separate employee injury report, open a workers' compensation claim, confirm the OSHA 300 log entry, and use debrief and peer support.

cards.front: What does New Jersey's Violence Prevention in Health Care Facilities Act require?
cards.back: A violence prevention committee with equal management and frontline representation, a risk assessment, a written prevention plan, staff training, a record of every violent incident, and protection from retaliation for reporting.

cards.front: Can an employer stop you from pressing charges after an assault?
cards.back: No. The decision is yours and retaliation is prohibited. New Jersey treats assault on a health care worker performing their duties as an elevated offense rather than simple assault.

cards.front: You find a patient on the floor. What are the first three actions?
cards.back: Stay with them and call for help, assess before moving for level of consciousness, deformity, pain, head strike, and limb movement, and stabilize the head if neck injury is possible.

cards.front: Why does anticoagulation change the plan after a fall with head strike?
cards.back: Patients on warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, or clopidogrel bleed intracranially with a normal initial exam, and it can declare itself hours later. They get imaging even when they look well.

cards.front: How do you document an unwitnessed fall?
cards.back: 'Found on the floor,' with exactly what you observed. 'Patient fell' claims a mechanism nobody saw. Add vitals, neuro checks, and a post-fall huddle within minutes.

cards.front: Where do wrong-patient errors actually originate?
cards.back: Duplicate medical records, similar names on one board, labels printed for the previous patient, and labeling at a workstation instead of at the bedside. The fix is labeling in the room, in the patient's presence.

cards.front: Why is 'wrong blood in tube' uniquely dangerous?
cards.back: The label is correct and the values are plausible, so no downstream check catches it. It is the mechanism behind fatal transfusion reactions, and bedside identification is the only barrier.

cards.front: What are the ED versions of a retained foreign object?
cards.back: A guidewire left in during central line placement, undocumented wound packing, a retained vaginal or nasal pack, and a broken catheter or needle fragment. Count and document what goes in.

cards.front: What is the difference between elopement and leaving against medical advice?
cards.back: Elopement is an at-risk patient leaving without staff knowing. Leaving AMA is a patient with capacity making a documented, informed choice. Only one of them is a safety event.

cards.front: What prevents elopement?
cards.back: Identify at-risk patients such as dementia, delirium, intoxication, psychiatric holds, children, and custody patients, then gown them, assign one-to-one observation, use door alarms, and place them visible from the desk.

cards.front: Which medication classes are 'high-alert' and why does the label use tall-man lettering?
cards.back: Insulin, opioids, anticoagulants, and concentrated electrolytes such as potassium chloride. Tall-man lettering such as hydrOXYzine versus hydrALAzine separates look-alike, sound-alike names.

cards.front: What is a sentinel event and what does it trigger?
cards.back: A patient safety event causing death, permanent harm, or severe temporary harm. It triggers a root cause analysis with an action plan, typically within 45 days.

cards.front: What does the New Jersey Patient Safety Act require, and what does it protect?
cards.back: Reporting serious preventable adverse events to the Department of Health within 5 business days, a root cause analysis and corrective plan within 45 days, and disclosure to the family. Self-critical analysis documents are shielded from discovery.

cards.front: Why is 'defend in place' usually the right fire strategy in a hospital?
cards.back: Hospitals are built as sealed compartments joined by fire doors, so a fire can burn in one compartment while people two doors away stay put. Moving ventilated and post-operative patients injures and kills.

cards.front: Who orders an evacuation, and what is the one exception?
cards.back: The incident commander or the fire officer in charge. The exception is immediate rescue: a patient in the room with the fire is moved now, without waiting for an order.

cards.front: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical evacuation?
cards.back: Horizontal moves patients through fire and smoke doors into the adjacent compartment on the same floor, and is tried first. Vertical goes down the stairs, never the elevator, and only when the floor is untenable.

cards.front: What equipment moves a bedbound patient down a stairwell?
cards.back: An evacuation sled or mattress sled strapped to the patient and slid down the stairs, a stair chair for anyone who can sit, and as a last resort a blanket drag or two-person carry.

cards.front: In what order are patients evacuated?
cards.back: Anyone in immediate danger first, then ambulatory patients who move themselves and clear the corridor, then wheelchair and assisted patients, then non-ambulatory total-care patients last.

cards.front: What has to happen to each room during an evacuation?
cards.back: It is cleared, marked on the door so no one searches it twice, and the patients are counted by name against the tracking board at the assembly point.

cards.front: What must happen before an oxygen zone valve is closed?
cards.back: An order from the person running the response, identification of every patient on piped oxygen in that zone, portable cylinders staged, and a bag-valve mask at the bedside of every ventilated patient.

cards.front: What are the four HICS sections and who sits above them?
cards.back: Operations, Planning, Logistics, and Finance and Administration, under the incident commander, who is supported by public information, safety, and liaison officers.

cards.front: What are job action sheets, plain language, span of control, and the labor pool?
cards.back: A printed card of duties per role; no color codes so outside agencies understand; 3 to 7 people per supervisor, ideally about 5; and off-duty staff report to the labor pool for assignment rather than to their own unit.

cards.front: Why are contaminated patients decontaminated before entering the ED?
cards.back: A contaminated patient brought inside contaminates the department and takes it out of service. Removing clothing alone eliminates roughly 80 to 90 percent of contaminant; the rest comes off with soap and water.

cards.front: What does ALARA mean and what are its three levers?
cards.back: As low as reasonably achievable, since no dose of scatter is known to be harmless. Time near the source, distance from it, and shielding with a 0.5 mm lead-equivalent apron and thyroid collar.

cards.front: What does the inverse square law mean for you at a portable X-ray?
cards.back: Dose falls with the square of distance: doubling your distance drops it to one quarter, tripling it to one ninth. Distance is the cheapest and strongest protection you have.

cards.front: Where do you stand for a portable film and for a C-arm?
cards.back: At least 6 feet away and about 90 degrees to the beam for a portable, because scatter is lowest perpendicular to it. With a C-arm, on the image-detector side, away from the under-table X-ray tube.

cards.front: Where is a dosimeter badge worn, and why there?
cards.back: At the collar, outside the lead apron, so it records what reaches the unshielded thyroid and eyes. A badge hidden under the apron understates your actual exposure.

cards.front: What are the occupational and pregnancy radiation dose limits?
cards.back: 50 mSv per year whole body. For a declared pregnant worker, 5 mSv for the entire pregnancy and about 0.5 mSv in any month. The lower limit starts only when the pregnancy is declared in writing.

cards.front: What is the most important fact about an MRI magnet?
cards.back: It is always on: overnight, between patients, and during a power failure. Nothing gets switched off when you walk in, so every screening rule applies at every hour.

cards.front: What are the four MRI zones?
cards.back: Zone I is public, Zone II is screening and interview, Zone III is restricted with controlled access where the field matters, and Zone IV is the magnet room itself.

cards.front: Which objects have become MRI projectiles?
