cards.back: Steel oxygen cylinders, IV poles, stretchers, trauma shears, stethoscopes, clipboards, pens, hairpins, and floor buffers. Oxygen entering Zone IV must be aluminum or piped.

cards.front: What does MRI screening specifically look for?
cards.back: Pacemakers and defibrillators, cochlear implants, neurostimulators, aneurysm clips, metal fragments in the eye from grinding or welding, medication patches with metallic backing that can burn, and any implant of unknown type.

cards.front: What do you do if a patient arrests inside the MRI scanner?
cards.back: Remove the patient from Zone IV to the designated resuscitation area and run the code there. The crash cart is ferromagnetic and never enters the magnet room.

cards.front: What is a quench and when is it used?
cards.back: An emergency dump of the magnet's liquid helium to kill the field, used only when a person is pinned by a ferromagnetic object. It destroys the magnet, displaces oxygen, and can cause frostbite, so the room is evacuated and ventilated.

cards.front: What are the three laser hazards in a procedure room?
cards.back: Eyes, needing wavelength-specific eyewear for everyone including the patient; plume, which carries viable virus such as HPV and needs smoke evacuation and high-filtration masks; and fire, so no alcohol prep and low oxygen near the beam.

cards.front: What is the 20-20-20 rule and how often do you replace work shoes?
cards.back: Every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds. Replace supportive shoes about every 6 months of full-time floor work, because the midsole compresses long before the tread looks worn.

cards.front: How long is caffeine's half-life, and what nap lengths work?
cards.back: About 5 hours, so stop roughly 6 hours before intended sleep. Nap 20 minutes to stay above deep sleep, or 90 minutes to complete a cycle. A 45-minute nap wakes you groggy out of slow-wave sleep.

cards.front: How impaired are you after a night shift?
cards.back: Being awake 17 hours impairs performance about like a blood alcohol of 0.05 percent, and 24 hours awake like 0.10 percent. The drive home is the most dangerous part of the shift.

cards.front: What separates burnout, compassion fatigue, and moral injury?
cards.back: Burnout is exhaustion, depersonalization, and lost accomplishment from workload. Compassion fatigue is secondary trauma from others' suffering. Moral injury is the damage from being required to act against what you know is right.

cards.front: What does the evidence say about psychological debriefing after a critical incident?
cards.back: Mandatory single-session psychological debriefing has not been shown to prevent PTSD and may worsen some people. Peer support programs and follow-up have better evidence; clinical team debriefs of the event are still useful.

cards.front: Why are eating and drinking prohibited in patient care areas?
cards.back: Bloodborne pathogen rules bar food, drink, cosmetics, and contact lens handling where exposure is reasonably likely, and specimens never share a refrigerator with food. A cup on a workstation is a real exposure route.

cards.front: Which deaths are reportable to the medical examiner in New Jersey?
cards.back: Violence including homicide, suicide, and accident; sudden death in apparent health; unattended death; suspicious circumstances; poisoning or overdose; occupational deaths; procedure or anesthesia related deaths; deaths in custody; public health threats; and unidentified remains.

cards.front: How is clothing cut off a possible homicide victim?
cards.back: Around the bullet or stab defects, never through them, because the size, shape, and residue of a defect carry forensic information. Then bag in paper, one item per bag, sealed and initialed.

cards.front: Why paper bags rather than plastic for evidence?
cards.back: Plastic traps moisture, letting bacteria degrade biological evidence. Wet or bloody clothing is air dried where possible and always bagged in paper, and clothing is never shaken out because trace evidence falls off.

cards.front: What does chain of custody actually require of you?
cards.back: Every transfer documented and signed with date and time, your initials across each seal, nothing left unattended on a counter, and nothing handed to family.

cards.front: What is the difference between pronouncement, certification, and release?
cards.back: A provider pronounces death and records the time. Certification is signing the cause on the death certificate, by the attending or the medical examiner. Release of the body to a funeral home is controlled by the medical examiner in their cases.

cards.front: How does New Jersey handle a religious objection to autopsy?
cards.back: An autopsy generally may not proceed over a known religious objection unless there is a compelling public necessity such as suspected homicide or a public health threat, and the family may seek a court's decision.

cards.front: Who is a mandatory reporter of suspected child abuse in New Jersey, and where do you call?
cards.back: Every person, with no exception for reporting through a supervisor. The State Central Registry at 1-877-NJ-ABUSE. The standard is reasonable suspicion, not proof, and you do not investigate.

quiz.q: Two patients on the same hallway grow carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella within four days of each other. What is the first correct action?
choices: Move both patients to a different hallway
Notify infection prevention so a case definition and line list can be started
Start empiric antibiotics on the neighboring patients
Switch the entire department to bleach wipes
quiz.why: Two unexpected cases in one place is enough to trigger an outbreak investigation, which begins with a case definition and line list. Moving patients or changing products before knowing the link addresses a mechanism nobody has identified yet, and prophylactic antibiotics are not an outbreak control measure.

quiz.q: A patient colonized with Candida auris is discharged. What is required for the room?
choices: A standard quaternary disinfectant on high-touch surfaces
Alcohol wipes on all equipment
A disinfectant specifically rated against Candida auris, plus attention to shared equipment that left the room
Soap and water followed by air drying
quiz.why: Candida auris resists several common quaternary products and persists on surfaces for weeks, so a product validated against it is required. Alcohol and washing do not eliminate it, and the cuffs, probes, and thermometers that left the room are as important as the room.

quiz.q: A visitor to a contact precautions room is handed a gown and gloves and walks in. Twenty minutes later you see her in the hallway still gloved. What was missed?
choices: A demonstration of how to remove the PPE before leaving the room
A signed visitor consent form
A surgical mask, which contact precautions require
Nothing, since visitors are not held to staff standards
quiz.why: Handing out PPE without showing the doffing sequence produces exactly this: contaminated gloves in a public corridor. Contact precautions do not require a mask, and visitors in a precaution room are held to the same barrier requirements as staff.

quiz.q: Which item belongs in a red regulated medical waste bag?
choices: A 4x4 gauze with a small dried blood spot
An empty saline flush syringe barrel
A used disposable blood pressure cuff
A suction canister full of liquid blood
quiz.why: Regulated waste is material saturated or dripping with blood or that would release it if compressed, which a full suction canister clearly is. A lightly stained gauze, an empty flush, and a cuff are regular waste, and over-red-bagging teaches staff the categories do not matter.

quiz.q: Single rooms are exhausted during a VRE outbreak. Which action is correct?
choices: Place a VRE patient with an MRSA patient, since both are on contact precautions
Place two VRE patients together with dedicated equipment for the room
Place a VRE patient with a patient who has no known colonization
Rotate patients through the same room between cleanings
quiz.why: Cohorting works only when the organism is identical, so two VRE patients can share a room. Pairing different organisms gives each patient the other's, pairing with an uncolonized patient creates a new case, and rotating without terminal cleaning spreads it further.

quiz.q: A patient in the waiting room is diagnosed with measles four hours after arrival. A tech with no documented immunity was unmasked in that room. What does she face?
choices: Azithromycin prophylaxis and continued work
A repeat IGRA in 8 to 10 weeks
MMR within 72 hours and exclusion from work from day 5 through day 21
VariZIG within 10 days and exclusion from day 8 through day 28
quiz.why: Non-immune measles exposure means MMR within 72 hours and a long exclusion spanning the infectious window of days 5 to 21. Azithromycin belongs to pertussis, IGRA to tuberculosis, and VariZIG with the day 8 to 28 exclusion to varicella.

quiz.q: A confirmed measles patient is moved out of triage room 2 at 1400. When can the next patient be placed in that room?
choices: Immediately after surface disinfection
After 24 hours
As soon as the door has been open for 10 minutes
After about 2 hours, because airborne particles remain suspended that long
quiz.why: Measles virus remains suspended in air for up to 2 hours after the patient leaves, so the room stays closed for that period regardless of surface cleaning. Opening the door earlier moves the aerosol into the corridor rather than clearing it.

quiz.q: A tech was in the room during intubation of a patient who turns out to have meningococcal meningitis. She was masked with a surgical mask and did not handle the airway. What is indicated?
choices: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg as a single dose
Rifampin for two days for everyone in the room
No prophylaxis, because she had no direct exposure to respiratory secretions
Immediate furlough for 21 days
quiz.why: Meningococcal prophylaxis targets staff with direct secretion exposure such as intubating, suctioning, or mouth-to-mouth, not everyone present. Blanket prophylaxis for a room drives resistance without benefit, and no work exclusion applies to meningococcus.

quiz.q: Which statement about post-exposure work restriction is correct?
choices: Pertussis exposure requires 21 days off regardless of symptoms
TB exposure requires exclusion until the 8 to 10 week retest
Varicella exposure in a non-immune worker means exclusion from day 8 through day 21, or day 28 if VariZIG was given
Influenza requires exclusion for 7 days from symptom onset
quiz.why: The varicella window reflects the incubation period, and VariZIG extends it by prolonging incubation. Pertussis-exposed staff work while asymptomatic on prophylaxis, TB-exposed staff keep working while tested, and influenza exclusion ends 24 hours after fever resolves without antipyretics.

quiz.q: Why is an interferon gamma release assay preferred over a skin test for TB screening in many health care workers?
choices: It gives a result in 15 minutes
It is not affected by prior BCG vaccination, which causes false-positive skin tests
It detects active disease rather than latent infection
It can be read without a return visit by the patient
quiz.why: BCG vaccination produces false-positive tuberculin skin tests, and the blood assay avoids that cross-reaction. It does not distinguish latent from active disease, which still requires symptoms and imaging, and it is a laboratory test rather than a rapid one.

quiz.q: An intubated, sedated patient begins reaching for the endotracheal tube and soft wrist restraints are applied. Which rules govern this?
choices: Behavioral restraint rules with a 1-hour face-to-face and a 4-hour order
Seclusion rules
No order is required because it protects a device
Non-violent medical restraint rules, with the order renewed per policy, typically each calendar day
quiz.why: The category is set by the purpose, and protecting a device or treatment is non-violent restraint. The 1-hour face-to-face and 4-hour order belong to violent or self-destructive behavior, and every restraint requires an order regardless of purpose.

quiz.q: A confused patient's stretcher is fitted with a lap belt she cannot unfasten. Staff call it a fall precaution. What is it actually?
choices: A restraint, because she cannot remove it herself
A fall precaution requiring no order
Seclusion
A chemical restraint
quiz.why: The test is whether the patient can freely release the device, and a belt she cannot undo confines her, which is the definition of restraint. Calling it a precaution does not change the requirement for an order and monitoring.

quiz.q: Behavioral restraints go on a 42-year-old at 2012. Which pair of times is correct?
choices: Face-to-face by 2112, order expires 0012
Face-to-face by 2212, order expires 2212
Face-to-face by 2042, order expires 2212
Face-to-face by 2112, order expires 0412
quiz.why: The face-to-face evaluation is due within 1 hour of application, so by 2112, and the adult behavioral order runs 4 hours, expiring at 0012. Two-hour limits apply to ages 9 to 17 and eight-hour orders do not exist in this framework.

quiz.q: Which restraint release criterion is written correctly?
choices: 'Release when calm'
'Release per provider discretion'
'Release when able to follow directions and no longer threatening staff'
'Release at end of shift'
quiz.why: Criteria must be behavioral and observable so anyone at the bedside can tell whether they have been met. Calm is unmeasurable, discretion names no behavior, and a clock time is unrelated to whether the danger has resolved.

quiz.q: A patient dies while in four-point behavioral restraints. What reporting is required?
choices: An internal log entry only, since restraint was ordered appropriately
A report only after a root cause analysis concludes restraint contributed
Notification to the medical examiner only
A report to CMS no later than close of business the next business day
quiz.why: Deaths occurring during restraint are reported to CMS by close of business the next business day, independent of any causation finding. The internal log option covers only soft two-point wrist restraints without seclusion, and medical examiner notification is a separate obligation.

quiz.q: A patient is confused, irritable, shouting, and has just thrown a urinal against the wall. Using the Broset checklist, how many of the six items are present and what does it mean?
choices: One item; document and reassess in an hour
Two items; low risk
Four items, well above the threshold of 2, meaning violence is likely and the team plans now
The checklist cannot be scored without a psychiatric evaluation
quiz.why: Confusion, irritability, boisterousness, and attacking objects are four of the six items, and a score above 2 predicts violence. The tool is designed for bedside scoring by trained staff, and waiting an hour with a score that high is how people get hurt.

quiz.q: A patient on a psychiatric hold arrives by police in street clothes carrying a backpack. What is the standard practice?
choices: Leave the belongings with the patient since police transported him
Change him into a gown and search and inventory belongings with security present and a witness
Search him alone to preserve his privacy
Store the backpack in the room within his reach
quiz.why: Police do not necessarily search for the hospital's purposes, and a bag within reach on a psychiatric hold is a weapon and ligature risk. Gowning with a witnessed, inventoried search is the standard, and a solo search leaves you alone with an unscreened patient.

quiz.q: A tech is punched, sustains a small facial laceration, is seen by a provider, gets three sutures, and returns to full duty. Which of the following is true?
choices: It is not OSHA 300 recordable because he returned to full duty
It is recordable only if he presses charges
It is recordable only if he misses a shift
It is OSHA 300 recordable because sutures are treatment beyond first aid
quiz.why: Recordability turns on whether treatment exceeded first aid, and sutures do. Return to duty, lost time, and criminal charges affect other columns and other processes but do not determine whether the case is recorded.

quiz.q: What does New Jersey's Violence Prevention in Health Care Facilities Act require of a covered hospital?
choices: Metal detectors at every entrance
Armed security officers on every shift
A violence prevention committee with equal labor and management representation, a risk assessment, a written plan, training, and a record of every violent incident
Automatic police notification for every reported incident
quiz.why: The Act builds a program: committee, assessment, written plan, training, incident records, and anti-retaliation protection. It does not mandate specific hardware such as metal detectors, specific staffing such as armed officers, or automatic police reporting, which remains the employee's choice.

quiz.q: An active shooter code is called. You are with a patient on a ventilator in a room off the main corridor. What is correct?
choices: Run to the nearest exit and leave the patient
Move into the hallway to see where the threat is
Secure in place: lock or barricade the door, lights off, phones silenced, out of sightline, open only for law enforcement
Disconnect the ventilator and carry the patient down the stairs
quiz.why: Hospitals add secure in place because ventilated patients cannot be run out. Entering the corridor for information places you in the threat's path, and disconnecting a ventilator to carry a patient down stairs is not survivable.

quiz.q: An 84-year-old on warfarin is found on the floor. She is alert, denies pain, and asks to get back in bed. What is correct?
choices: Assist her up and document no injury
Recheck her in one hour and image only if she becomes symptomatic
Document the event as a witnessed fall based on her account
Assess before moving her, and expect head imaging because she is anticoagulated even though she looks well
quiz.why: Intracranial bleeding on warfarin frequently presents hours later with a normal initial exam, so the medication and mechanism drive imaging rather than her appearance. Moving before assessment risks worsening injury, and a fall no one saw is documented as found on the floor.

quiz.q: A tube of blood labeled for patient A actually contains patient B's blood. Why is this the most dangerous specimen error?
choices: It causes hemolysis, which delays the result
The analyzer will reject it
Nothing downstream can detect it, because the label matches and the values look plausible
It is detected at the blood bank crossmatch every time
quiz.why: There is no automated catch for an identity error: label, order, and result all appear consistent. Crossmatch compares the labeled sample to donor units, so it confirms compatibility with the wrong person's blood, which is the mechanism behind fatal transfusion reactions.

quiz.q: A patient with dementia who was waiting for placement is no longer in his room. His clothes are gone. What is this and what happens first?
choices: Leaving against medical advice; document his choice
Elopement; notify the charge nurse and security immediately and activate the facility's code
A discharge that was not documented; call the family
Nothing until an hour has passed to see if he returns
quiz.why: An at-risk patient leaving without staff knowledge is elopement, not an informed refusal, because dementia removes the capacity that AMA presumes. The response is immediate notification and a search, since delay is what turns elopement into a never event.

quiz.q: Which is an ED version of a retained foreign object?
choices: A guidewire left in place during central line insertion
An IV catheter that infiltrated
A dressing changed less often than ordered
A splint applied too tightly
quiz.why: A retained guidewire is a classic never event and can embolize or require surgical retrieval. Infiltration, dressing frequency, and a tight splint are complications or care issues, not objects left inside the patient.

quiz.q: You nearly hand a nurse the wrong patient's specimen labels, catch it yourself, and no patient is affected. What should happen?
choices: Nothing, since no harm occurred
Chart in the patient's record that a near miss occurred
Tell your supervisor verbally and take no further action
File a near-miss safety report so the labeling workflow flaw is examined
quiz.why: Near misses are free information about a defense that nearly failed, and the system fix comes from the report. Incident reports never go in the patient's chart, and a verbal mention leaves no record for the committee that could change the workflow.

quiz.q: Under the New Jersey Patient Safety Act, what protection does a facility receive in exchange for reporting?
choices: Immunity from all malpractice claims arising from the event
Confidentiality protection for the self-critical analysis documents, shielding them from discovery
A waiver of the 45-day root cause analysis requirement
Exemption from disclosing the event to the patient or family
quiz.why: The privilege attaches to the self-critical analysis materials, which is what makes candid internal investigation possible. It is not immunity from suit, the 45-day analysis is still required, and disclosure to the patient or family remains mandatory.

quiz.q: A fire is confirmed in a storage room two compartments away. The alarm is sounding and no evacuation order has been given. What do you do?
choices: Close doors, account for your patients, and hold in place pending the incident commander's decision
Begin moving your patients down the nearest stairwell
Open the fire doors so staff can move faster
Close the oxygen zone valve for your hallway
quiz.why: Compartmentalization means defend in place is the designed response, and the evacuation decision belongs to the incident commander. Propping fire doors defeats the compartment, and closing a zone valve without an order cuts oxygen to ventilated patients.

quiz.q: Vertical evacuation is ordered from your floor. Which is the correct sequence of patients?
choices: Total-care patients first, since they take the longest
Alphabetical by room to avoid missing anyone
Whoever is closest to the stairwell
Anyone in immediate danger, then ambulatory patients, then assisted, then total-care
quiz.why: Immediate danger always comes first, then ambulatory patients who move themselves and clear the corridor for slower groups. Starting with total-care patients consumes all available staff while dozens who could walk remain in danger.

quiz.q: The incident commander orders an oxygen zone valve closed because of a fire. What must happen first?
choices: Nothing; the valve closes immediately on the order
Identify every patient on piped oxygen in that zone, stage portable cylinders, and place a bag-valve mask at every ventilated patient's bedside
Notify respiratory therapy after the valve is closed
Increase all patients' flow rates before closing
quiz.why: Closing the valve instantly removes oxygen and ventilator gas from every patient behind it, so alternatives must be at the bedside before it turns. Notifying afterward leaves a gap, and raising flow rates beforehand feeds the fire without helping anyone.

quiz.q: Which statement about the hospital incident command system is correct?
choices: Color codes are used so information stays confidential from outside agencies
Job action sheets tell each assigned role exactly what to do, and span of control runs 3 to 7 people
Off-duty staff should report directly to their own units
The incident commander personally assigns every individual task
quiz.why: HICS standardizes roles with printed job action sheets and keeps supervisors within a workable span of control. It uses plain language precisely so outside agencies understand, and arriving staff report to the labor pool rather than self-deploying.

quiz.q: A patient covered in an unknown industrial chemical arrives by private car and walks toward the triage door. What is correct?
choices: Bring him straight to a treatment room and start decontamination there
Have him wait in the waiting room until the decon team is assembled
Send him back out to be transported by EMS
Stop him outside, begin decontamination before entry, starting with clothing removal
quiz.why: A contaminated patient brought inside contaminates the department and removes it from service. Clothing removal alone eliminates roughly 80 to 90 percent of contaminant, so decon starts outside immediately rather than in a room or a waiting area.

quiz.q: You must stay in the room during a portable chest X-ray to hold a combative patient's arm. What is correct?
choices: Stand at the head of the bed in line with the beam wearing an apron
Wear apron, thyroid collar, and leaded gloves, keep every part of yourself out of the primary beam, and stand perpendicular to it
Hold without shielding, since the exposure is brief
Ask the technologist to increase the exposure so it takes less time
quiz.why: Shielding plus staying out of the primary beam is the requirement, and scatter is lowest at 90 degrees to the beam. Brevity does not justify skipping shielding under ALARA, and increasing technique raises both patient and scatter dose.

quiz.q: During a C-arm fluoroscopy reduction, where is scatter dose highest?
choices: On the image-detector side above the patient
On the X-ray tube side, typically low and beneath the table
Uniformly distributed throughout the room
Behind the lead-lined control booth
quiz.why: Scatter comes off the patient back toward the tube, which sits under the table, making the low tube side the hottest position. Dose is never uniform in a room, and the control booth exists precisely because it is shielded.

quiz.q: Where should a dosimeter badge be worn by a tech who wears a lead apron?
choices: At the waist under the apron
In a pocket, since position does not matter
On the apron's back, away from the source
At the collar outside the apron
quiz.why: The collar position outside the apron measures dose to the unshielded thyroid, eyes, and head, which is what the limit is meant to protect. A badge under the apron or in a pocket reports a shielded, falsely low number.

quiz.q: You are asked to bring a patient to MRI at 0200 when no scans are running. What applies?
choices: The magnet is always on, so full screening of the patient, the equipment, and yourself applies
Screening can be abbreviated because the magnet is idle
Ferromagnetic items are safe if kept more than 3 feet from the bore
The magnet can be powered down briefly for an urgent transfer
quiz.why: A superconducting magnet holds its field continuously, including overnight and during power failures, so the hazard never pauses. Distance does not make a steel cylinder safe, and the only way to kill the field is a quench, which is an emergency destruction of the magnet.

quiz.q: A patient becomes unresponsive and pulseless inside the MRI bore. What is the correct action?
choices: Start compressions in the bore and call the code to Zone IV
Quench the magnet, then resuscitate at the scanner
Remove the patient from Zone IV to the designated resuscitation area and run the code there
Wait for the MRI safety officer before touching the patient
quiz.why: The crash cart, monitor, and laryngoscope are ferromagnetic and cannot enter the magnet room, so the patient comes out to the resuscitation area. Quenching wastes minutes, destroys the magnet, and creates an oxygen displacement hazard, and waiting for an officer costs perfusion.

quiz.q: During a laser procedure, which practice is correct?
choices: Everyone including the patient wears eyewear rated for that laser's specific wavelength
Standard safety glasses protect against any laser
Alcohol-based skin prep is acceptable if applied thinly
Laser plume is harmless because the tissue is vaporized
quiz.why: Protective eyewear is wavelength specific and covers everyone in the room, patient included. Standard glasses offer no protection, alcohol prep near a laser is an ignition source regardless of thickness, and plume carries viable virus and carcinogens requiring smoke evacuation.

quiz.q: A tech finishes a 12-hour night at 0730, feels fine, and has a 45-minute drive. She has been awake 20 hours. What is the safest advice?
choices: Coffee for the road and drive now
Drive with the window down and music on
Take surface streets to reduce speed
Nap first or arrange a ride, because 17 hours awake impairs performance like a blood alcohol of 0.05 percent
quiz.why: Sleep-deprivation impairment is measurable and self-assessment is unreliable, which is why feeling fine at 20 hours awake means nothing. Caffeine masks sleepiness without restoring vigilance, and air, music, and slower roads do not reverse microsleeps.

quiz.q: You have 50 minutes between patients on a night shift and want to nap. What is the best plan?
choices: Sleep the full 50 minutes for maximum rest
Sleep about 20 minutes to stay above deep sleep and wake alert
Skip the nap, since anything under an hour is useless
Drink coffee at the start of the nap and sleep 45 minutes
quiz.why: A 20-minute nap stays out of slow-wave sleep and avoids sleep inertia, while roughly 45 to 50 minutes reliably wakes you groggy mid-cycle. Short naps measurably improve alertness, so skipping is worse than napping briefly.

quiz.q: A tech says she is not tired, she is furious, because she spent the shift doing what the department's constraints demanded rather than what her patients needed. What is the most accurate term?
choices: Compassion fatigue
Burnout
Moral injury
Secondary traumatic stress
quiz.why: Moral injury is the harm from being required to act against your own judgment of what is right, and anger rather than exhaustion is the tell. Burnout centers on exhaustion and depersonalization from workload, while compassion fatigue and secondary traumatic stress come from exposure to others' trauma.

quiz.q: Which statement about support after a critical incident is best supported by evidence?
choices: Mandatory single-session psychological debriefing prevents PTSD
Peer support programs and follow-up have better evidence than a single mandatory debriefing session
Staff who show no reaction within 24 hours will not have one
Employee assistance programs report attendance to your manager
quiz.why: Single-session mandatory psychological debriefing has not been shown to prevent PTSD and may harm some participants, while peer support has better evidence. Delayed reactions days to weeks later are the norm, and employee assistance programs are confidential by design.

quiz.q: A young man dies of a gunshot wound. His shirt must be removed. What is correct?
choices: Cut through the bullet holes to save time and note their location
Place the wet shirt in a sealed plastic bag to contain blood
Give the clothing to the family with the belongings
Cut around the defects, preserve them intact, and bag the shirt in paper
quiz.why: The size, shape, and residue around a defect carry range and weapon information that cutting through destroys. Plastic traps moisture and degrades biological evidence, and evidence in a medical examiner case never goes to the family.

quiz.q: Which death would NOT ordinarily be reported to the New Jersey medical examiner?
choices: A suspected fentanyl overdose
A death two days after a fall at a construction site
A death during induction of anesthesia
An expected death from metastatic cancer in a hospice patient under a physician's active care
quiz.why: An expected death from a known disease with an attending physician available to certify the cause falls outside the reportable categories. Overdose, occupational injury, and procedure or anesthesia related deaths are all explicitly reportable.

quiz.q: A family states that their religion forbids autopsy and that burial must occur before sundown. The death is an unwitnessed cardiac arrest in a 70-year-old with known heart disease. What is your role?
choices: Tell them autopsy is mandatory in all medical examiner cases
Promise them no autopsy will be performed
Communicate the objection to the nurse and provider immediately so it reaches the medical examiner within the family's timeline
Direct them to file a court motion
quiz.why: New Jersey recognizes religious objections to autopsy absent a compelling public necessity, so the objection must reach the decision makers fast. You neither grant nor deny it, and sending a grieving family to court as a first step wastes the hours they have.

quiz.q: Which action correctly maintains chain of custody?
choices: Sealing each item in its own bag, labeling it, initialing across the seal, and documenting a signed transfer with date and time
Placing all clothing in one bag and leaving it at the nurses' station for the detective
Handing belongings to the patient's brother with a receipt
Photographing the items and then discarding the soiled ones
quiz.why: Custody requires individually sealed, initialed items and a documented, signed transfer at every step. Combining items mixes trace evidence, unattended bags break the chain, and family handoff or disposal destroys it entirely.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old dies after an injury whose history changes twice. In New Jersey, what is your personal obligation?
choices: Report your reasonable suspicion to the State Central Registry yourself
Report only if the attending physician agrees the history is implausible
Document your concern and let the charge nurse decide
Investigate and gather evidence before reporting anything
quiz.why: New Jersey has universal mandatory reporting, making the duty personal and non-delegable. The threshold is reasonable suspicion rather than proof or consensus, and investigating is the agency's role, not the reporter's.

scenarios.title: Smoke in the corridor outside CT
scenarios.intro: 0247. You are pushing a stretcher back from CT with a 71-year-old woman who has a hip fracture, `4 L/min` by nasal cannula from a portable E cylinder, and an IV running. Halfway down the connector corridor you smell smoke, and you see a haze near the ceiling coming from an equipment alcove about thirty feet ahead of you. There is a fire door between you and the alcove, currently propped open with a wedge. The nearest patient room door is ten feet behind you.

steps.prompt: You are alone with one patient, smoke visible ahead, and a propped fire door between you and it. What do you do first?

choices.text: Move the patient back away from the alcove, kick the wedge out so the fire door closes, then pull the nearest alarm station
choices.feedback: Correct order. Rescue means getting your patient out of immediate danger first, and closing that fire door is the single highest-value action available to you because it restores the compartment the building was designed around. Alarm comes right behind it.

choices.text: Leave the stretcher where it is and run ahead to see how big the fire is
choices.feedback: You have just abandoned a patient on oxygen in a smoke-filling corridor to gather information you do not need. Size-up happens after people are out of danger, and never by leaving a patient alone.

choices.text: Pull the alarm first, then come back for the patient
choices.feedback: Defensible but out of order. RACE puts rescue first, and here rescue plus closing the propped fire door takes about eight seconds and buys the whole corridor time. Then alarm.

choices.text: Grab the extinguisher off the wall and attack the alcove
choices.feedback: You have a patient on an oxygen cylinder attached to you, no alarm sounded, and no one knows where you are. Extinguish is the last letter of RACE for a reason, and never with a patient in tow.

steps.prompt: The fire door is closed and the alarm is sounding. You have moved the patient back through a second set of doors into the adjacent compartment, where the charge nurse and two other techs are gathering. Your patient is anxious and her oxygen cylinder gauge reads `700 psi`. The charge nurse asks you for a status.

choices.text: Report the location and what you saw, state that the fire door is now closed, and flag that her E cylinder is at 700 psi and will last about 125 minutes at 4 L/min
choices.feedback: Exactly what a charge nurse needs: location, what you did, and a resource number she does not have to calculate. (700 minus 200) times 0.28 divided by 4 is about 35, so roughly 35 minutes, not 125 - and knowing the real figure is the point of the formula.

choices.text: Report the location and what you saw, state the fire door is closed, and say the cylinder is at 700 psi and you need a replacement soon
choices.feedback: Clean and correct. You gave position, action taken, and a concrete resource need. At 4 L/min a 700 psi E cylinder gives roughly 35 minutes, so 'soon' is accurate and a fresh tank should be staged now.

choices.text: Say everything is fine and wait for instructions
choices.feedback: You are the only person who has seen the fire. Withholding that leaves the charge nurse building a plan on nothing, and the oxygen problem arrives in half an hour with no warning.

choices.text: Hand off the patient and go back to help fight the fire
choices.feedback: Untrained freelancing during a fire response is how people get hurt and how the accountability count breaks. Stay with your assignment until someone with the incident command role reassigns you.

steps.prompt: The house supervisor assumes incident commander and announces over the radio that the department is holding in place for now, with horizontal evacuation of the CT corridor zone only. She asks you to take one hallway and clear it. Six patients: two ambulatory, two in wheelchairs, one bedbound on a ventilator, and one in restraints.

choices.text: Move the ventilated patient first, since he is the most vulnerable
choices.feedback: Understandable instinct, wrong sequence. The ventilated patient consumes three or four staff and several minutes. Doing him first leaves five people including two who could have walked out in ten seconds still sitting in the zone.

choices.text: Direct the two ambulatory patients through the fire doors now, then the wheelchairs, then organize help for the ventilated and restrained patients
choices.feedback: Correct. Ambulatory patients move themselves, clear the corridor, and free you for the patients who need bodies. The two complex patients then get the staff they actually require.

choices.text: Clear the rooms in numerical order to avoid missing anyone
choices.feedback: Room order is a counting strategy, not a triage strategy. You mark rooms as cleared to avoid missing anyone; you move patients in order of danger and mobility.

choices.text: Release the restrained patient first so he can walk out on his own
choices.feedback: Releasing behavioral restraints in the middle of an evacuation, without an assessment or an order, creates a second emergency inside the first. He moves with staff, restrained, under the same rules.

steps.prompt: Five patients are out. The ventilated patient is being moved with three staff and a bag-valve mask at the bedside. Over the radio you hear that the fire officer is considering closing the oxygen zone valve for the CT corridor. A colleague standing next to the valve asks you whether she should just close it now to be safe.

choices.text: Tell her yes, closing it is always the safer choice in a fire
choices.feedback: No. That valve feeds the ventilated patient who is still in the zone. 'Safer' without knowing who is behind the valve is how a fire response kills someone who was never near the fire.

choices.text: Tell her not to touch it until the incident commander orders it, and that the ventilated patient in that zone needs to be out or bagged first
choices.feedback: Right on both counts. The valve closes only on command, and the precondition is that every patient behind it has portable oxygen or a bag-valve mask at the bedside.

choices.text: Tell her to close it but turn it back on in a few minutes
choices.feedback: Cycling a zone valve is not a thing. Restoring piped gas involves pressure checks and is not a switch you flip back on, and the interruption still reaches every patient in the zone.

choices.text: Tell her you do not know and to ask the charge nurse
choices.feedback: Safe, but you do know. Deferring a question you can answer correctly slows the response, and in this case the correct answer is short: not without the order, not before the ventilator patient is covered.

steps.prompt: The alcove fire is out. It was an electrical fault in a charger cabinet. The incident commander asks every zone for a patient accounting before anyone returns. You had six patients in your hallway.

choices.text: Report six patients by name, matched against the tracking board, and confirm each room was marked cleared
choices.feedback: This is the number that ends the incident. Names against the board, not a headcount, and the door markings prove nobody is left behind a closed door in a smoke-filled zone.

choices.text: Report 'all six accounted for' from memory
choices.feedback: Memory under stress is exactly what the tracking board exists to replace. A count from memory feels identical whether it is right or wrong, and that is the problem.

choices.text: Report that the hallway is empty and you saw everyone leave
choices.feedback: An empty hallway is not an accounting. Patients end up in bathrooms, in stairwells, and in the wrong assembly area, which is why reconciliation is by name against a list.

choices.text: Start returning patients to their rooms while the count is being compiled
choices.feedback: Moving people back while the accounting is still open guarantees a miscount and sends patients into a zone that has not been declared safe. Wait for the all clear.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: **rescue, close the door, alarm, contain, and only then anything heroic.** Closing one propped fire door was the highest-value thing you did all night, because hospitals survive fires by compartment, not by extinguisher. Evacuation order follows mobility, not sympathy: immediate danger, ambulatory, assisted, total care. The oxygen zone valve is never yours to close, and it never closes before every patient behind it has a portable cylinder or a bag-valve mask at the bedside. And the incident does not end when the fire is out. It ends when every patient is accounted for by name against a written list.

scenarios.title: The rash in chair 6
scenarios.intro:
1105 on a Tuesday. The waiting room is full: twenty-two people, including two infants in carriers and an older man on home oxygen. You are doing waiting room reassessments.

Chair 6 is a 23-year-old man, unaccompanied, here for 'fever and a rash.' He has been in the waiting room since `0840`. He is coughing, his eyes are red and watering, and he has a blotchy red rash that he says started on his face yesterday and is now moving down his chest. He tells you he just got back from a trip abroad nine days ago and does not think he ever got 'the baby shots.'

steps.prompt: You have four facts: fever with rash spreading head downward, conjunctivitis, cough, recent international travel, and no vaccination history. What is the immediate action?

choices.text: Put a surgical mask on him, move him out of the waiting room to a separate space, and tell the charge nurse you suspect measles
choices.feedback: Correct and urgent. Cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and a cephalocaudal rash in an unvaccinated traveler is measles until proven otherwise. Source control plus removal from a shared airspace is the only thing that limits the exposure list.

choices.text: Move him to the front of the triage line and take a full set of vitals in the open triage bay
choices.feedback: You sped up his care and kept him in shared air. An open triage bay is a second waiting room with better lighting. Mask and separate first, assess second.

choices.text: Put an N95 on him so he cannot transmit
choices.feedback: Wrong direction. Patients get surgical masks for source control; staff wear the N95. An N95 on a febrile, coughing patient is uncomfortable, unnecessary, and takes one out of your stock.

choices.text: Tell him to wait outside the building until a room is available
choices.feedback: Sending a febrile, potentially measles-infected patient outside unmonitored is abandonment, and it does nothing about the two hours he already spent in the waiting room. He needs a controlled space inside.

steps.prompt: He is masked and standing with you in a side corridor. The charge nurse asks what you need. There is one negative-pressure room, currently empty.

choices.text: Ask for the negative-pressure room, tell her you will don an N95 before going in, and ask her to notify infection prevention now
choices.feedback: All three pieces. The room addresses the route, the respirator addresses you, and infection prevention needs the call early because the contact list is already two hours long.

choices.text: Ask for any private room with the door closed
choices.feedback: A closed door does not stop an airborne pathogen; measles travels on air currents through doorways and stays suspended for 2 hours. It has to be the negative-pressure room.

choices.text: Ask for the negative-pressure room and go in with a surgical mask, since you feel well
choices.feedback: A surgical mask does nothing against measles. This is the exposure that puts you on a 17-day work exclusion if your immunity is not documented.

choices.text: Ask for the negative-pressure room and check your own immunization record before entering
choices.feedback: Reasonable and worth doing, but the room and the N95 come first, and infection prevention needs to be called now rather than after you look up your records.

steps.prompt: He is in the negative-pressure room with the door closed. You are outside in the corridor. Infection prevention calls back and asks you to help reconstruct the exposure: who was in the waiting room, and what happened to the space he occupied.

choices.text: Tell them approximately how many people were there and that the chair has been wiped down
choices.feedback: Wiping a chair addresses a route measles does not use, and 'approximately' is not a contact list. They need names and times, and the room needs to stay closed.

choices.text: Give them his arrival time of 0840, direct them to the tracking board and registration log for everyone present since then, and report that the waiting room needs to be handled as an airborne exposure space
choices.feedback: That is the reconstruction they need: a start time, a source of names, and the correct hazard framing. The exposure window runs from his arrival, not from when someone suspected it.

choices.text: Tell them only the patients seated near him were exposed
choices.feedback: Measles is not a proximity disease. Airborne particles fill the room and persist for 2 hours, which is why everyone who shared the space during and after his time there is on the list.

choices.text: Give them his arrival time and offer to start calling patients yourself
choices.feedback: The arrival time is the right contribution. Notification is infection prevention's job with a scripted message, and a well-meaning call from a tech creates confusion and wrong information.

steps.prompt: Infection prevention asks whether you have documented immunity to measles. You check: your file shows one MMR dose as a child and nothing since. You feel fine.

choices.text: Tell them one documented dose, which is not presumptive immunity, and ask about MMR within 72 hours and the work exclusion window
choices.feedback: Honest and correct. Presumptive immunity is two documented doses, a positive titer, or lab-confirmed disease. One dose puts you in the post-exposure pathway: vaccine within 72 hours, and exclusion from day 5 through day 21.

choices.text: Tell them you are immune, since you had a dose as a child
choices.feedback: One dose is not presumptive immunity, and misreporting it protects your schedule at the cost of every patient you see for the next three weeks. This is the moment where honesty is the clinical act.

choices.text: Say you are not sure and will check later
choices.feedback: The interventions are on a clock measured in hours: MMR within 72 hours, immune globulin within 6 days. 'Later' is how people miss both windows.

choices.text: Tell them one dose, and ask whether a titer drawn today could establish immunity
choices.feedback: A reasonable question and some programs will draw one, but do not let the titer delay the vaccine decision. The 72-hour window keeps running while the result is pending.

steps.prompt: He is moved to an inpatient airborne room three hours later. A colleague, annoyed at the disruption, says loudly at the desk: 'It's probably just a virus, everybody overreacted.'

choices.text: Agree, to keep the peace on a busy shift
choices.feedback: The next time someone with a rash and a cough shows up, that agreement is what stops the mask from going on. Silence in the face of that sentence has a cost you never get to see.

choices.text: Say plainly that measles hangs in the air for 2 hours, that two infants were in that waiting room, and that this is exactly the response the policy is built for
choices.feedback: Short, factual, and it names the stakes without a lecture. The infants in the waiting room are the reason, and saying it out loud is what keeps the next response fast.

choices.text: Say nothing but document the exposure carefully
choices.feedback: The documentation matters and you should do it. But culture is built by what gets said at the desk, and letting that sentence stand unchallenged shapes how the next case is handled.

choices.text: Report the colleague to the manager for undermining infection control
choices.feedback: Escalating a desk comment to management skips the cheap, effective step of correcting it directly, and it costs you the working relationship you need for the rest of the shift.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: **fever plus rash plus travel plus no vaccines equals mask and remove, before anything else.** Measles is airborne, stays suspended for `2 hours`, and the exposure list starts at the patient's arrival time, not at the moment someone got suspicious. A surgical mask on the patient controls the source; an N95 on you is the only thing that protects you, and a closed ordinary door protects no one. Know your own immunization status before you need it, because one MMR dose is not presumptive immunity and the price of that gap is seventeen days off. And when someone at the desk calls the response an overreaction, the two infants in the waiting room are your answer.

scenarios.title: Found on the floor in room 12
scenarios.intro:
1930. Room 12 holds an 84-year-old woman, admitted through the ED four hours ago for weakness and a urinary tract infection. She takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. She has a yellow fall-risk band. She was last seen `25 minutes` ago, sitting up, waiting for a bed upstairs.

You walk in with her dinner tray and find her on the floor beside the stretcher, on her right side, awake, embarrassed, saying 'I was only going to the bathroom, please just help me up.'

steps.prompt: She is awake and talking, asking to be helped up. There is a small area of redness over her right temple. What do you do?

choices.text: Help her back onto the stretcher quickly so she is not on a cold floor, then call the nurse
choices.feedback: The floor is uncomfortable, not dangerous; moving her before assessment is. An occult hip fracture or cervical injury gets worse with an untrained lift, and once she is back in bed the exam has lost its information.

choices.text: Stay with her, call for help without leaving, and assess before moving: level of consciousness, pain, deformity, movement of all four limbs, and that temple
choices.feedback: Correct on every count. You do not leave her, you do not move her, and you gather the findings that determine whether this becomes a spine precaution and a CT rather than a lift.

choices.text: Go get the nurse and the lift equipment
choices.feedback: Leaving her alone on the floor is how a second fall attempt happens while you are down the hall. Call out or use the call bell; do not walk away from a patient on the ground.

choices.text: Ask her what happened and document her account before doing anything else
choices.feedback: Her account matters and you will take it, but not before you have confirmed she is not injured. Assessment first, history alongside it, and the chart still says found on the floor because nobody saw it.

steps.prompt: The nurse arrives. The patient moves all four limbs, has no neck pain, no hip pain, and no deformity. She says she does not know whether she hit her head, but the temple redness is new. She is oriented to person and place, not to the day.

choices.text: Report the findings and specifically flag that she is on apixaban with a possible head strike
choices.feedback: That is the sentence that changes the plan. Anticoagulation plus possible head strike means imaging regardless of how well she looks, and it is the detail most likely to get lost in a busy handoff.

choices.text: Report that she is uninjured and help her up now that the nurse is here
choices.feedback: You have declared an outcome you cannot know. An intracranial bleed on apixaban can be entirely silent for hours, and calling her uninjured closes a door that should stay open.

choices.text: Note that she is confused and attribute it to her urinary tract infection
choices.feedback: Plausible and possibly true, and also exactly how a head bleed gets missed in an older patient. Baseline confusion from infection does not excuse you from evaluating a new head strike on an anticoagulant.

choices.text: Report the findings and suggest a set of neuro checks
choices.feedback: Neuro checks are appropriate and will be ordered. But the driving fact is the anticoagulant, and saying that out loud is what triggers imaging rather than watchful waiting.

steps.prompt: She is back on the stretcher with two staff and a slide sheet, a head CT is ordered, and the provider has seen her. The nurse asks you to document your part.

choices.text: Chart: 'Patient fell while attempting to ambulate to the bathroom.'
choices.feedback: You did not see a fall. Writing a mechanism you did not witness puts an unverified claim into the permanent record, and it may be contradicted by the imaging or by her own later account.

choices.text: Chart: 'Found on floor at 1930, right lateral, awake and verbal, area of redness right temple, moves all four extremities, denies neck and hip pain. Nurse and provider notified. Assisted to stretcher with two staff and slide sheet.'
choices.feedback: Objective, timed, and limited to what you observed. 'Found on floor' is the honest description of an unwitnessed event, and the rest is findings rather than conclusions.

choices.text: Chart: 'Patient found on floor. Incident report filed.'
choices.feedback: The first half is right. The second half never belongs in a patient's chart: the incident report is a separate, protected quality document, and referencing it pulls it toward the medical record.

choices.text: Chart the findings and add that the patient states she was going to the bathroom
choices.feedback: Acceptable, as long as it is clearly attributed to her as a statement rather than written as fact. Quoted patient accounts are fine; narrated mechanisms you did not see are not.

steps.prompt: The charge nurse calls a post-fall huddle at the bedside: you, the nurse, and the provider, four minutes long. She asks what contributed.

choices.text: Say you do not know, since nobody saw it
choices.feedback: The huddle is not asking you to reconstruct the fall. It is asking what was in the room. You have that information and it is the whole point of doing this within minutes rather than at a committee next month.

choices.text: Report what you actually saw in the room: bed height, whether the call bell was in reach, whether she had non-skid socks, when she was last toileted, and how long she had been waiting for a bed
choices.feedback: That is exactly the data the huddle exists to collect, and it is only available now. Most falls happen on the way to a bathroom, so the toileting interval is often the finding that changes practice.

choices.text: Suggest raising all four side rails to prevent a recurrence
choices.feedback: Four rails up is a restraint and an entrapment hazard, and patients climb over them and fall from a greater height. The answer is proactive toileting, a bed alarm, and visibility, not confinement.

choices.text: Say the fall was unavoidable because she is confused
choices.feedback: Confusion is a risk factor, not an explanation, and calling a fall unavoidable ends the analysis before it starts. The huddle is looking for the modifiable pieces.

steps.prompt: The CT shows a small subdural hematoma. She is admitted to a monitored bed. A colleague says: 'Well, at least you found her fast. No point filling out the report now, the CT already tells the story.'

choices.text: Agree; the clinical documentation covers it
choices.feedback: The chart records what happened to her. It does not record that the bed was at the wrong height, that nobody had toileted her in two hours, or that she had waited four hours for a bed. Only the safety report carries that.

choices.text: File the safety event report anyway, covering the contributing conditions, because the chart and the report do different jobs
choices.feedback: Right. The medical record documents the patient's care; the safety report feeds the system analysis, and a fall with injury on an anticoagulant is exactly the event a committee needs to see.

choices.text: File the report but copy the clinical note into it
choices.feedback: Better than nothing, but the value is in the conditions, not the clinical findings. Write what the room looked like and what the workflow was, because that is what the committee cannot get anywhere else.

choices.text: Wait to file until the patient's outcome is known
choices.feedback: Reports are filed at the time, while details are accurate and recoverable. Waiting on an outcome delays the system fix and degrades the information you are trying to preserve.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: **assess before you lift, and let the anticoagulant drive the plan.** An 84-year-old on apixaban with a possible head strike gets imaged even when she is alert, oriented, and embarrassed, because the bleed declares itself hours later. An unwitnessed fall is charted as **found on the floor**, with findings rather than conclusions, and the incident report is never mentioned in the chart. The post-fall huddle happens in minutes because the room still holds the evidence: bed height, call bell, socks, and the toileting interval that most falls trace back to. And the safety report gets filed even when the clinical story is fully documented, because the chart records what happened to the patient while the report records what the system let happen.
